items.title: Le rôle du partenariat public-privé dans le développement des infrastructures en Guinée (Par Kikala Camara)
items.description: Routes, ponts, ouvrages d’assainissement, logements, équipements publics, infrastructures énergétiques et logistiques : le développement économique de la Guinée nécessite des investissements considérables dans les infrastructures. Face à l’ampleur de ces besoins, l’État ne peut cependant pas toujours compter uniquement sur les ressources budgétaires publiques pour financer, construire et entretenir l’ensemble des infrastructures nécessaires au développement du pays. C’est dans ce contexte que le partenariat public-privé (PPP) peut constituer un instrument stratégique, à condition d’être bien préparé, bien négocié et rigoureusement suivi. Le PPP : associer la vision publique à la capacité du secteur privé Un partenariat public-privé permet à l’État et au secteur privé de travailler ensemble autour d’un projet d’intérêt général. L’État définit les priorités, protège l’intérêt général et fixe les exigences de service public. Le partenaire privé peut, selon le montage retenu, apporter des financements, son expertise technique, ses capacités de réalisation, d’exploitation ou de maintenance. L’objectif n’est donc pas de remplacer l’État par le privé. Il s’agit plutôt de mobiliser les capacités des deux parties autour d’objectifs clairement définis. Accélérer la réalisation des infrastructures Les besoins de la Guinée sont importants, particulièrement dans les infrastructures routières, l’assainissement, l’énergie, les transports, l’immobilier et les équipements collectifs. Dans certains cas, les PPP peuvent permettre de mobiliser plus rapidement des capitaux et des compétences pour réaliser des projets qui seraient difficiles à financer immédiatement et entièrement sur le budget de l’État. Cette approche est particulièrement intéressante pour les infrastructures susceptibles de générer des revenus ou de s'inscrire dans un modèle économique durable. La volonté de recourir davantage à ces mécanismes est déjà visible. Les autorités guinéennes envisagent notamment des montages PPP et d'autres mécanismes de financement innovants pour certains grands projets routiers. Le secteur privé national doit également trouver sa place Le développement des PPP en Guinée doit aussi constituer une opportunité pour renforcer les entreprises guinéennes. Les grands projets ne devraient pas seulement permettre de construire des infrastructures. Ils devraient également contribuer au transfert de compétences, à la création d’emplois, à la formation des jeunes ingénieurs et techniciens et au développement d’entreprises nationales capables, demain, de participer à des projets encore plus importants. Il faut donc favoriser, dans le respect des règles de concurrence et des exigences de qualité, des mécanismes permettant aux entreprises locales compétentes de participer à ces projets, directement ou en partenariat avec des groupes internationaux. L’objectif doit être double : construire les infrastructures dont la Guinée a besoin et construire simultanément une expertise guinéenne durable. Le PPP n’est toutefois pas une solution miracle Il serait également dangereux de considérer le partenariat public-privé comme une source de financement gratuite. Quel que soit le montage choisi, quelqu’un doit supporter le coût de l’infrastructure : l’État, les usagers, le partenaire privé à travers les risques qu’il assume, ou une combinaison de ces acteurs. Un mauvais PPP peut engager les finances publiques pendant de nombreuses années. C’est pourquoi chaque projet doit faire l’objet d’études sérieuses avant sa contractualisation. Il faut notamment déterminer si le PPP offre réellement un meilleur rapport coût-performance qu'un financement public classique, identifier les risques et définir clairement qui doit les supporter. Transparence, compétence et contrôle : trois conditions indispensables Pour réussir une politique de PPP, trois principes me paraissent fondamentaux. Le premier est la transparence . Les procédures de sélection et les engagements contractuels doivent être suffisamment clairs pour protéger l’intérêt public. Le deuxième est la compétence technique et financière . Négocier un contrat portant sur plusieurs centaines de milliards de francs guinéens et pouvant s’étendre sur plusieurs décennies nécessite des équipes publiques hautement qualifiées. Le troisième est le contrôle de la performance . Une fois le contrat signé, l’État doit disposer des capacités nécessaires pour vérifier la qualité des travaux, les délais, les coûts, la maintenance et les niveaux de service prévus. Un PPP performant n’est pas simplement un contrat signé : c’est un partenariat dont les résultats sont mesurés pendant toute sa durée. Penser également à l’entretien des infrastructures L’un des grands avantages potentiels du PPP est de pouvoir intégrer la maintenance dès la conception du projet. Construire une route ou un ouvrage est une chose. Garantir son bon fonctionnement pendant quinze, vingt ou trente ans en est une autre. Notre réflexion sur les infrastructures doit donc progressivement évoluer du simple coût de construction vers le coût du cycle de vie de l’ouvrage . Une infrastructure moins chère à construire mais coûteuse à entretenir n’est pas nécessairement une bonne opération pour l’État. Faire des PPP un véritable instrument de développement La Guinée connaît aujourd’hui une phase importante de transformation économique et infrastructurelle. Cette dynamique représente une opportunité pour repenser la manière dont nous finançons, réalisons et entretenons nos infrastructures. Le partenariat public-privé peut jouer un rôle majeur dans cette transformation s’il repose sur des projets économiquement pertinents, des études solides, des contrats équilibrés, une véritable transparence et une administration capable de défendre durablement les intérêts de l’État. Le véritable enjeu n’est donc pas de multiplier les PPP. Il est de sélectionner les bons projets, avec les bons partenaires, selon les bons montages et avec une exigence permanente de résultats. Car au-delà du financement, la réussite des infrastructures guinéennes dépendra toujours de trois choses : la vision, la compétence et la qualité de l’exécution. Kikala Camara, ingénieur et manager de projets L’article Le rôle du partenariat public-privé dans le développement des infrastructures en Guinée (Par Kikala Camara) est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Daily Insight for CEOs: Attracting and retaining critical talent
items.description: Insight. Talent is one of the organization’s most important competitive assets. CEOs must understand which skills and people are critical to delivering the strategy and create an environment where high-performing talent can thrive. Competitive compensation matters, but talented people also seek purpose, growth, recognition, meaningful responsibility, and effective leadership. Retention begins with understanding why valuable people stay—and why they leave. Key Strategies: 1. Identify mission-critical talent. 2. Strengthen employee development. 3. Create meaningful career pathways. 4. Recognize high performance. 5. Build an engaging leadership culture. CEO Leadership Actions. Review critical talent risks. Engage directly with key leaders and high-potential employees. Ensure the organisation offers meaningful development opportunities. Actionable Tip. Ask your HR and executive teams to identify the five roles where losing the current incumbent would create the greatest organisational risk. Why This Matters? Retaining critical talent protects organisational knowledge, continuity, productivity, and competitive advantage. About the Author. Ernest De-Graft Egyir, CEO advisor, Thought Leader and Founding CEO of Chief Executives Network Ghana, convenes the Ghana CEO Summit and served on Ghana’s Economic Dialogue Planning Committee.

items.title: Les États-Unis affirment disposer de capacités militaires en orbite
items.description: Le secrétaire américain à la Force aérienne, Troy Meink, a révélé hier, lundi 14 septembre, que les États-Unis disposaient « d'armes de contrôle spatial en orbite capables de défendre les forces interarmées contre toute action hostile d'un adversaire » U.S. Admits It Has Weapons In Orbit », TWZ , 14 septembre 2026.'> 1 . Il s'agit de la première fois que l'armée américaine reconnaît disposer d'armes déployées en orbite. Les propos de Meink s'apparentent à un avertissement lancé à la Russie et à la Chine, qui investissent également pour renforcer leurs programmes militaires spatiaux. Plusieurs experts, dont le chercheur au CSIS Clayton Swope, considèrent toutefois que les propos de Meink sont trop « vagues » pour dissuader efficacement Moscou et Pékin US military reveals it has weapons in space », Financial Times , 15 septembre 2026.'> 2 . Ce dernier a en effet refusé de préciser de quelles capacités les États-Unis disposaient, et s’est contenté de déclarer que les « mesures prises » par Washington visaient à « conserver sa suprématie dans l’espace ». Selon un responsable américain, ces capacités pourraient permettre aux États-Unis de détruire un satellite ennemi « s'il était utilisé pour cibler des troupes américaines ou un satellite américain » U.S. has deployed first space-based weapon, Air Force secretary says », The Washington Post , 14 septembre 2026.'> 3 . Victoria Samson, directrice de la sécurité et de la stabilité spatiales à la Secure World Foundation, considère quant à elle qu’il s’agirait plutôt de brouilleurs, une arme non cinétique qui permet de neutraliser un satellite sans créer de débris Publication de Victoria Samson sur X , 14 septembre 2026.'> 4 . Ces capacités pourraient aussi constituer la première étape du Golden Dome de Donald Trump, Meink ayant déclaré qu’il existait désormais du matériel prêt à l’emploi pour des intercepteurs spatiaux. L’armée américaine considère que l’accès à l’espace et son utilisation relèvent « d’un intérêt national vital », et cite explicitement la Chine et la Russie comme les deux principales puissances qui menacent le développement des capacités américaines. Cette annonce pourrait accélérer la course aux armes spatiales. Washington estime que l’Armée populaire de libération développe ses propres capacités spatiales et anti-spatiales pour être capable de mener des frappes de précision à longue portée et de bloquer les communications spatiales satellitaires d’autres armées. Les renseignements américains considèrent également que Moscou « mène des activités de recherche, de développement, d’essai et de déploiement de systèmes anti-spatiaux afin de tirer parti de la vulnérabilité perçue de la dépendance militaire américaine vis-à-vis de l’espace » Space Threat Fact Sheet , U.S. Space Force, juillet 2026.'> 5 . En avril, le commandant du U.S. Space Command, Stephen Whiting, avait déclaré que la Russie avait déployé des armes antisatellites opérationnelles visant des satellites américains US Space Command : Russia is now operationalizing co-orbital ASAT weapons », Ars Technica , 23 avril 2026.'> 6 . Au même moment, l’armée américaine s’entraînait lors d’un exercice de simulation à faire face à l'utilisation par Moscou de sa « capacité antisatellite nucléaire présumée » A Russian space nuke was focus of US wargame, Space Command says », Defense One , 14 avril 2026.'> 7 . L’article Les États-Unis affirment disposer de capacités militaires en orbite est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: A Diagnosis for Social Conflict That Gets Lost Along the Way
items.description: Weddings, famously, create conflict. Before I got married, my parents and I fought over the guest list. A friend of mine struggled with adding some of her husband’s Protestant traditions to their otherwise Jewish ceremony. Another friend had to decode, and then manage, complicated tensions among her future aunts- and uncles-in-law. All of these issues got resolved, and according to the conflict-resolution facilitator Priya Parker, the process of figuring them out made our weddings more successful expressions of our values. Parker explored the group creation of meaning in her 2018 best seller, The Art of Gathering . In her new book, The Art of Fighting , she writes that arguments are crucial to a group’s ability to do just that. What’s more, in American society—which Parker describes as both conflict averse and low on big rituals—high-stakes events such as weddings are among the “last remaining collective mechanisms to help us have the fights we need to have to figure out who we are now.” The Art of Fighting is predicated on Parker’s conviction that without confrontation, no group can work well. “Fighting,” she writes in her prologue, “is not the death of community. It is its lifeblood.” Parker considers Americans far too willing to focus on themselves rather than their communities, in large part due to a widespread fear of confrontation. A lot of loneliness, in her view, originates from the all-too-common decision to exit a challenging situation instead of dealing with its simmering disagreements. It’s a smart diagnosis, one that’s as relevant to small-bore social scenarios as it is to interactions within religious organizations, schools, and workplaces. The choice to hide from conflict is, to Parker, in many situations, a choice to be alone. Parker’s idea that conflict is inherently a social good is intriguing and counterintuitive. But The Art of Fighting is not nearly as communitarian a book as its setup would suggest. Although its more abstract passages describe healthy confrontation as helpful and worthy, its examples tell another story. Parker presents The Art of Fighting as a “group-help book” but tends to take a side in her case studies—and in most instances, her side wins. [ Read: A wedding reveals how much help is really available to you ] Her own life serves as illustration, too, and often provides the book’s most revealing moments. By way of arguing that everyone needs to get comfortable with disagreement, she mentions a clash she and her father had after the latter got upset that Parker hadn’t invited her stepbrother’s wife to her baby shower. As Parker relates it, their discussion of her reasoning—she and her stepsister-in-law just aren’t close—ends not with compromise or reconciliation but with the blunt lines: “He wasn’t getting it. And that was OK.” Such a one-sided resolution suggests a disinterest in compromise and an interpretation of fighting as an individualistic act. Facing conflict may very well be a social good—I believe it is—but her book more often seems to urge readers to wade into arguments to get what they want. The Art of Fighting is full of stories of conflict. Some appear only once, and some are threaded throughout the book. The quarreling groups that Parker features, many of which she worked with in her role as a facilitator, range in size from an extended family to a percussion ensemble to a large architecture firm. Parker uses every case to ask a variation of her central question: “How do you fight with those to whom you want to belong?” In the book’s most moving example, she writes about a church that, in the mid-1990s, deliberated about and then voted on whether it would perform and recognize gay marriages. Its pastor, Martin Copenhaver, understood that they couldn’t make a decision that might lead to division if his church were to survive. “In the political arena,” he tells Parker, “if you win by one vote, you win. In this arena, you win by one vote, you don’t win.” Hoping to forge meaningful consensus, he hosted four meetings to discuss the subject; only those who attended were allowed to vote. After the election—the church decided, not unanimously but with “no great division,” to allow gay marriage—he asked everyone to reconcile in person with someone who voted differently. In essence, Copenhaver organized the entire conflict to prioritize congregants’ investment in the church, not to lead them toward a certain outcome. I wanted to learn more about how other sorts of disputes, especially less orchestrated ones, might bolster a sense of community. But Parker is surprisingly blurry about the variety of incentives for confronting or ignoring tension that exist in one setting or another. Some strategies for managing conflict—waiting to engage until no one has steam pouring from their ears; ensuring that the arguing parties’ grievances and goals are clear; creating the right conditions for a tough conversation—may apply to all kinds of groups. [ Read: Why are we so spiteful? ] But the book doesn’t do enough to acknowledge that different sorts of conflicts have different stakes. Starting a fight for the good of the group may be wise among relatives but foolish if doing so could also mean losing your job. And a values-based argument may not be worthwhile in a corporate context where the overall goal is to maximize profit. One of Parker’s recurring examples is a debate that took place within a law firm about whether the TV in its common space should show World Cup games played in Qatar. It begins with an intern objecting, on Slack, to the “human rights abuses of workers in the lead up to the World Cup and the horrific status of rights for LGBTQ people and women in Qatar.” The managing partners invited employees to what Parker characterizes as a too-wide conversation about the World Cup. It was, she writes, “the wrong fight with the wrong assemblage of people in the wrong room.” Parker uses this argument to underscore good and bad ways to navigate conflicts, especially ones that arise online—certainly an important issue in our screen-heavy times. But missing from this analysis is any real engagement on Parker’s part with the substance of the conflict itself. Readers never learn how the issue was resolved: Did the World Cup get shown or not? Was there ever a meaningful discussion about the objections the intern had raised? The book uses this example to describe strategies for handling internal dissent, focusing on how the managing partners could best have reestablished peace among their employees. It becomes a story about conflict management rather than conflict as a potential social good. Some of Parker’s personal anecdotes more vividly illustrate her not-quite-communitarian approach to fighting. In one, she describes enrolling her children and their cousin in a small soccer camp one summer. Initially, the kids report hating camp and getting bullied by their counselors. Parker speaks with the camp director, who talks with his employees and establishes that Parker’s children and niece, who started on the eighth week of camp, are unfamiliar with both the established cohort’s “teasing culture” and the basic rules of soccer. Parker suggests that the camp’s coaches “give our kids a Week One experience, orient them, do the things you did with all the other kids when they were new.” They comply, and the camp—which Parker needs for child care—works out. Parker’s reaction to the situation is entirely reasonable; what parent wouldn’t try to help a kid who’s being picked on, or scramble to rescue a child-care setup that seems about to fail? It is not, however, an illustration of confrontation as community service. She shows herself engaging in conflict to get her kids special treatment rather than nudging the kids to advocate for themselves or asking how the camp might better help them settle in despite their latecomer status. Another way to put this is that no compromise is on offer here, and we get no sense of a group working together. Parker, as the customer, gets to be right. Throughout The Art of Fighting , individuals prevail in this way. A woman named Rebekah, exhausted by attending her family’s Passover seders—too much cooking, too much disruption to routine, too much airtime for her right-wing uncle—gives them up. But Parker never writes about what Rebekah’s parents, siblings, or children might lose when she and her nuclear family stop coming, or how her continued, if conflicted, attendance might have led her relatives to create more sustainable traditions. Just as some therapists prioritize clients over the other people in their lives, Parker prioritizes the subjects of her anecdotes over those with whom they fight. What these stories add up to, ultimately, is a much less surprising take on conflict than the book tries to lay out. Parker provides a useful guide to having arguments in good faith without hurting anyone’s feelings unnecessarily or creating a corporate crisis. But arguments can be so much more than that. Alone in the book, the story of Copenhaver’s church demonstrates that even enduring and loaded disagreements can, if handled with enough care and respect, strengthen the bonds between parties—in other words, they can be productive, not just nondestructive. Many readers will have experienced this in intimate relationships. I, for one, have grown closer to some friends after air-clearing arguments and have drifted from others who weren’t willing or able to talk through issues when they arose. But as Parker points out, public life in the United States isn’t set up for healthy conflict. Meaningful group fights are rare experiences. Aside from my wedding planning, I haven’t been part of one. I believe, in theory, that such a dispute could be transformational for both a community and its individual members. But in order for Parker’s book to have taught me how to navigate one, she would have had to truly let go of the old idea that the reason to fight is to win.

items.title: Ghana launches initiative to cut maternal deaths by 20% annually
items.description: Ghana has launched the Presidential Initiative on Maternal Health Emergency Response (PRIMER) to step up efforts to reduce maternal deaths and ensure women receive timely and quality care before, during, and after childbirth. The five-year multisectoral initiative was launched on September 15 by Vice President Prof. Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang on behalf of President John Dramani Mahama under the theme; “No Woman Should Die While Giving Life”. Speaking at the launch, Prof. Opoku-Agyemang noted that Ghana’s maternal mortality ratio remained above the Sustainable Development Goal target of fewer than 70 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030. She said PRIMER would bring together ministries, public institutions, local authorities, traditional and religious leaders, civil society, the private sector and communities to address the challenges that continue to affect maternal survival. Deputy Minister for Health, Prof. Grace Ayensu-Danquah, revealed that the Ministry had made its Maternal Mortality Action and Response Programme (MMARP) the fifth pillar of PRIMER, giving the initiative a dedicated clinical and operational component. Prof. Ayensu-Danquah indicated that Ghana’s maternal mortality ratio currently stands at about 234 deaths per 100,000 live births, while institutional maternal deaths reached 965 in 2025. She attributed a significant proportion of the deaths to referrals from lower-level facilities. Among the challenges are the late identification of high-risk pregnancies, delays in emergency referrals, inadequate critical-care equipment and limited access to blood and other essential resources. Prof. Ayensu-Danquah said MMARP would focus on strengthening primary-level care, referral systems, and emergency response, with the goal of reducing maternal mortality by 20 percent annually over the next three years. The vice president urged health professionals, communities, traditional and religious leaders, development partners, and relevant government institutions to play their respective roles in ensuring that women seek care early and receive timely interventions.

items.title: Houet : Le Cabinet médical privé Bien-Être situé au quartier Yéguéré de Bobo-Dioulasso fermé pour manquements
items.description: Houet : Le Cabinet médical privé Bien-Être situé au quartier Yéguéré de Bobo-Dioulasso fermé pour manquements Bobo-Dioulasso, 15 sept. 2026 (AIB) – La police municipale de Bobo-Dioulasso a procédé, le vendredi 11 septembre 2026, à la fermeture du Cabinet médical Bien-Être, situé au quartier Yéguéré, pour des manquements relevés par les services compétents. L’opération, conduite par l’Inspecteur de police municipale et Directeur de la police de la salubrité et de la tranquillité urbaine, Yaya Séré, intervient après un premier passage des forces de l’ordre effectué le jeudi 10 septembre 2026. « Cette fermeture fait suite aux réquisitions de l’autorité communale et des autorités sanitaires », a-t-il expliqué. Selon lui, les mesures font notamment suite au non-respect de l’arrêté conjoint n°2006-111 portant classification et nomenclature des structures privées sanitaires. Des contrôles effectués par la Direction régionale de la santé ont permis de relever plusieurs insuffisances au sein du cabinet. Il s’agit notamment de la présence d’un laboratoire, d’une salle de consultation, d’un service de planification familiale et d’un dépôt pharmaceutique dans des conditions jugées non conformes aux exigences réglementaires applicables aux structures sanitaires privées. Les services compétents ont également relevé des préoccupations en matière d’hygiène et de salubrité, notamment la vétusté et l’accessibilité difficile des latrines, ainsi que la présence de tas d’ordures et de dépotoirs aux alentours de la structure. À l’issue de l’opération, un procès-verbal de fermeture a été établi. Le Cabinet médical Bien-Être restera fermé jusqu’à nouvel ordre, en attendant les instructions de l’autorité compétente. Sa réouverture sera subordonnée à la prise en compte des recommandations de la Direction régionale de la santé et au respect des exigences réglementaires en vigueur. Yaya Séré a invité les promoteurs des structures sanitaires privées à se conformer aux normes en matière de santé, d’hygiène et de salubrité. Agence d'Information du Burkina AB/wis

items.title: Hammamet accueille le championnat d’Afrique de golf 2026
items.description: La Fédération tunisienne de golf (FTG), créée en 1992, va accueillir pour la première fois de son histoire les plus grands golfeurs du continent africain au golf Citrus à Hammamet, pour le Championnat d’Afrique de golf, du 14 au 17 octobre 2026. Ce sera un grand rendez-vous pour tous les joueurs amateurs de golf sur le sol africain soucieux de réaliser un bon chemin pouvant les mener au circuit pro. L’édition tunisienne connaitra un nombre record de participants avec la présence de 19 pays (Algérie, Botswana, Cameroun, Egypte, Gabon, Ghana, Kenya, Libye, Ile Maurice, Maroc, Réunion, Afrique du Sud, Seychelles, Sierra Leone, Tanzanie, Ouganda, Zambie, Zimbabwe et Tunisie). La Tunisie accueillera par la même occasion l’assemblée générale de la Confédération africaine de golf (CAG) qui se tiendra le vendredi 16 octobre a Hammamet et qui devra élire le nouveau bureau exécutif de l’instance africaine pour le mandat 2026-2030. Outre les dirigeants du golf en Afrique, bon nombre d’invités parmi les responsables du golf mondial seront également présents. Appelée à défendre les couleurs nationales à cet important rendez-vous, la sélection tunisienne poursuit sa préparation au Golf Citrus Hammamet. Rabeh Bedoui, Baha Boulakmine et Aziz Dardouri effectuent des séances quotidiennes sous la férule de l’entraineur national Hatem Nasr, alors que Mehdi Ben Youssef se prépare d’arrache pied aux Etats-Unis afin d’être fin prêt le jour J. Le comité d’organisation est, lui aussi, au four et au moulin ces derniers temps en vue d’assurer le meilleur séjour possible aux hôtes de la Tunisie ainsi que le succès à cet événement sportif continental. Une conférence de presse se tiendra pour présenter l’événement est prévue le 14 octobre au Golf Citrus, juste avant le démarrage des compétitions. I. B. L’article Hammamet accueille le championnat d’Afrique de golf 2026 est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Banwa : les appelés de l’immersion patriotique s’engagent dans la lutte contre le paludisme
items.description: Banwa : les appelés de l’immersion patriotique s’engagent dans la lutte contre le paludisme Solenzo, 15 sept. 2026 (AIB)-Les appelés de l’immersion patriotique obligatoire ont participé le lundi 14 septembre 2026 à une opération de destruction des gîtes larvaires et de salubrité autour et à l’intérieur du Centre de santé et de promotion sociale (CSPS) urbain 2 de Solenzo. Cette opération s’inscrit dans le cadre de leur engagement patriotique en faveur de la santé et du bien-être des populations. Elle a consisté notamment au nettoyage des abords du CSPS, de l’intérieur de la cour ainsi qu’à l’élimination des endroits susceptibles de favoriser la prolifération des moustiques vecteurs du paludisme. Munis de matériels de nettoyage, les appelés ont procédé au ramassage des déchets, au désherbage et à l’assainissement des différents espaces du centre de santé. Selon le porte-parole des appelés, Élie Saboué cette opération est un appel à la population de veiller à l'environnement. « Si le CSPS est plein d'herbes qui cachent des moustiques, si on ne fait rien les malades ne vont pas guérir et aussi les voisins du CSPS tomberont malades à cause des moustiques. C'est pourquoi nous avons décidé de venir nettoyer car la propreté est un remède » a-t-il affirmé. Selon ce dernier l'activité traduit également leur volonté de mettre en pratique les valeurs de civisme, de solidarité et de service à la communauté inculquées au cours de l’immersion patriotique obligatoire. Agence d'Information du Burkina SO/wis

items.title: Mines : NMC et Glencore concluent un accord de plus de 300 millions $ pour 50 à 60 millions de tonnes de bauxite guinéenne
items.description: © ADOBESTOCK " data-large-file="https://i0.wp.com/mediaguinee.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_8581.jpeg?fit=1024%2C683&ssl=1" /> La Nimba Mining Company S.A (NMC), entreprise entièrement détenue par l’État guinéen, et le groupe Glencore ont conclu un accord d’offtake portant sur le préfinancement et la commercialisation de la production de bauxite de NMC, selon un communiqué publié à cet effet. D’après le communiqué, l’accord a été signé le 7 septembre 2026 à Paris, à l’issue d’un appel d’offres international. Il prévoit un préfinancement de plus de 300 millions de dollars ainsi que la commercialisation de 10 à 12 millions de tonnes de bauxite par an pendant cinq ans. Sur la durée du contrat, le volume engagé devrait ainsi atteindre 50 à 60 millions de tonnes de bauxite, soit une moyenne comprise entre 830 000 et 1 million de tonnes par mois, précise le document. Pour NMC, cet accord offre une meilleure visibilité sur les volumes de vente et les flux financiers sur une période de cinq ans, en reliant la montée en puissance de sa production à des débouchés commerciaux identifiés, selon la même source. Le communiqué souligne également que cet accord intervient alors que la Guinée entend accélérer la transformation locale de sa bauxite. Trois raffineries d’alumine sont actuellement en construction dans le pays. Leur mise en service doit permettre de transformer une part croissante du minerai en alumine, ouvrant ainsi la voie, à terme, à une production nationale d’aluminium. « L’accord d’offtake conclu entre Nimba Mining Company – entreprise à capitaux entièrement publics – et Glencore ne constitue pas une simple transaction commerciale. Il marque une étape décisive dans la stratégie minière de l’État guinéen et s’inscrit pleinement dans le Programme Simandou 2040 », a déclaré, dans le communiqué, Djiba Diakité, président du Comité stratégique de Simandou. Il ajoute que la Guinée entend « peser sur les conditions de valorisation de ses ressources, sécuriser la commercialisation de sa bauxite, accélérer sa transformation sur le sol national et bâtir avec ses partenaires des relations à bénéfices partagés ». De son côté, Bouna Sylla, ministre des Mines et de la Géologie, salue un accord qui, selon lui, témoigne de la confiance placée en la Guinée dans le cadre du Programme Simandou 2040. « Cet investissement dans Nimba Mining Company (NMC), réalisé avec l’appui du Comité stratégique de Simandou, témoigne de la confiance placée en la République de Guinée à travers le Programme Simandou 2040, vision de Son Excellence Mamadi Doumbouya, Président de la République », a-t-il déclaré. Le ministre estime également que cet accord marque « le début d’une coopération de long terme avec Glencore ». « Nous nous réjouissons que Glencore, l’une des premières compagnies minières mondiales, place sa confiance en la Guinée et mette son expertise internationale au service du développement de notre secteur minier, au bénéfice de l’ensemble de la population guinéenne et de toutes les parties prenantes », a ajouté Bouna Sylla. Mediaguinee L’article Mines : NMC et Glencore concluent un accord de plus de 300 millions $ pour 50 à 60 millions de tonnes de bauxite guinéenne est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: 18e Sommet des BRICS : Le Président Xi Jinping participe à la première session et prononce une allocution importante
items.description: Dans l’après-midi du 12 septembre 2026, le Président chinois Xi Jinping a participé à la première session du 18 e Sommet des BRICS à New Delhi et a prononcé une allocution importante intitulée Assumer ensemble les responsabilités de notre époque pour être une force pionnière. Au cours des 20 ans écoulés, le BRICS n’a cessé de se développer avec une vitalité et une dynamique forte, devenant la plateforme de coopération la plus influente au monde pour les marchés émergents et les pays en développement. Le Président chinois Xi Jinping l’a indiqué dans une allocution importante intitulée Assumer ensemble les responsabilités de notre époque pour être une force pionnière prononcée à la première session du 18 e Sommet des BRICS à New Delhi. « Ce sont 20 ans d’indépendance et de développement. Les pays du BRICS ont exploré activement une voie de développement adaptée à leurs conditions nationales, donnant l’exemple du renforcement collectif des marchés émergents et des pays en développement. Ce sont 20 ans de solidarité éprouvée. Les pays du BRICS ont répondu ensemble aux défis tels que la crise financière internationale, l’épidémie de COVID-19 et le changement climatique et défendu fermement les intérêts communs du Sud global, apportant de la stabilité et des énergies positives à notre monde. Ce sont 20 ans de coopération fructueuse. Les BRICS ont réalisé un élargissement historique, mis en place une architecture de coopération multidimensionnelle et aux différents niveaux, ouvrant une nouvelle phase du développement de qualité d’une coopération BRICS plus vaste », a-t-il déclaré. Le Président Xi Jinping a souligné par ailleurs qu’à l’heure de l’accélération des changements inédits depuis un siècle, le Sud global gagne en puissance et l’avènement d’un monde multipolaire devient irrésistible. « Dans le même temps, nous assistons à la montée de l’unilatéralisme et de la politique du plus fort, au bouleversement du multilatéralisme et de l’ordre international et au creusement des déficits de paix, de développement, de sécurité et de gouvernance. Les pays du BRICS doivent se tenir fermement du bon côté de l’Histoire et agir en tant que force pionnière de notre époque pour faire évoluer l’ordre international dans un sens plus juste et plus équitable et construire ensemble une communauté d’avenir partagé pour l’humanité », a-t-il estimé. Le président chinois a appelé les pays du BRICS à être pionniers dans la promotion du développement innovant. « Nous, pays du BRICS, devons garder l’initiative entre nos mains, renforcer la coopération en matière d’IA et encourager l’open source, l’ouverture, la coopération et le partage, ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives à notre coopération pragmatique et la porter à une nouvelle hauteur. La Chine sera heureuse de voir les pays du BRICS prendre une part active dans l’Organisation mondiale de la coopération en matière d’IA. La Chine lance l’Initiative du BRICS pour une IA au service de l’industrialisation de type nouveau et est prête à travailler ensemble avec toutes les parties pour remporter plus de fruits en matière de R&D et d’application et approfondir la coopération sur les chaînes industrielles et d’approvisionnement », a-t-il déclaré. Préserver la paix et la stabilité Xi Jinping a également appelé les pays du BRICS à être pionniers dans la préservation de la paix et de la stabilité. « Nous devons porter la vision de sécurité commune, intégrée, coopérative et durable, rejeter la mentalité de la guerre froide et la confrontation des blocs et nous opposer à la violation de la souveraineté et à l’ingérence dans les affaires intérieures d’autrui. Nous devons participer de manière constructive au règlement des dossiers brûlants et apporter une contribution unique des BRICS à la recherche des solutions qui s’attaquent à la fois aux symptômes et aux racines des problèmes. La Chine entend travailler avec les autres pays membres du BRICS à jouer le rôle qui leur revient pour réaliser la paix et la tranquillité au Moyen-Orient », a-t-il soutenu. Le président chinois a aussi invité les pays du BRICS à être pionniers dans la promotion de l’inspiration mutuelle entre civilisations. « Nous devons faire rayonner les valeurs communes de l’humanité et plaider pour les échanges, l’inspiration mutuelle et la coexistence harmonieuse entre civilisations. Nous devons valoriser le Forum du BRICS sur les échanges humains et culturels pour partager les expériences en matière de gouvernance et dégager des énergies positives pour un développement stable des relations entre les pays du monde. Il nous faut approfondir la coopération culturelle, touristique et éducative, intensifier les échanges entre nos jeunes et favoriser les visites dans les deux sens pour renforcer la compréhension mutuelle et l’amitié entre nos peuples », a-t-il déclaré. En marge du Sommet, les dirigeants des pays du BRICS ont visité une exposition de photos commémorant le 20e anniversaire du BRICS, planté ensemble des arbres et pris une photo de famille. " data-large-file="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-15-at-10.57.41.jpeg" class="size-full wp-image-169596" src="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-15-at-10.57.41.jpeg" alt="" width="600" height="325" srcset="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-15-at-10.57.41.jpeg 600w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-15-at-10.57.41-300x163.jpeg 300w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-15-at-10.57.41-150x81.jpeg 150w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 600px) 100vw, 600px" /> En marge du Sommet, les dirigeants des pays du BRICS ont visité une exposition de photos commémorant le 20e anniversaire du BRICS, planté ensemble des arbres et pris une photo de famille. De l’avis du président Xi, les pays du BRICS doivent être pionniers dans la réforme et le perfectionnement de la gouvernance mondiale. « Nous devons suivre la tendance générale de la démocratisation des relations internationales, œuvrer à la construction d’un système de gouvernance mondiale plus juste et plus équitable et défendre l’autorité des Nations Unies. Nous devons soutenir le système commercial multilatéral centré sur l’Organisation mondiale du commerce et rejeter toute forme de mesures protectionnistes. Nous devons orienter la gouvernance mondiale sur les nouvelles frontières telles que le cyberespace, l’espace extra-atmosphérique et la mer profonde pour accroître le droit à la parole des pays du Sud global », a-t-il noté. Le Président Xi Jinping a par ailleurs appelé à continuer de faire preuve de sincérité, rechercher le terrain d’entente par-delà les divergences, respecter les préoccupations vitales de part et d’autre, et favoriser la compréhension mutuelle et gérer adéquatement les divergences à travers la communication et le dialogue pour assurer un développement solide et de long terme de la coopération BRICS. « La Chine assumera la présidence du BRICS l’année prochaine et tiendra le 19 e Sommet des BRICS. Elle est prête à travailler ensemble avec toutes les parties à bâtir le consensus et à envisager l’avenir en vue d’inaugurer une troisième décennie d’or de la coopération BRICS et à ouvrir des perspectives radieuses de prospérité et de progrès partagés », a-t-il laissé entendre. Les différentes parties ont hautement salué les accomplissements que le BRICS a réalisés dans son développement depuis sa création il y a 20 ans, considérant que le BRICS est doté d’une large représentativité et recèle un énorme potentiel de développement. Elles ont affirmé que face à l’intensification des conflits géopolitiques et à la montée de l’unilatéralisme, les pays du BRICS avaient des responsabilités à assumer pour faire entendre la voix du Sud global, défendre le multilatéralisme, soutenir le rôle central des Nations Unies, préserver l’égalité souveraine de tous les pays, respecter le droit international, s’opposer à l’ingérence dans les affaires intérieures d’autrui, soutenir le libre-échange et répondre ensemble aux défis planétaires. Elles ont souligné la nécessité pour les différentes parties de faire valoir l’esprit du BRICS, d’approfondir leur coopération dans différents domaines, de renforcer la résilience économique et d’œuvrer à l’avènement d’un ordre international plus juste et plus inclusif et à la construction d’un monde multipolaire sûr et prospère. Elles ont salué la contribution importante apportée par la Chine au développement et au renforcement du BRICS et exprimé leur soutien à la présidence chinoise pour l’organisation du 19 e Sommet des BRICS en 2027 en vue de porter ensemble la coopération BRICS à de nouvelles hauteurs. Le Sommet a adopté la Déclaration de New Delhi du 18 e Sommet des BRICS. Synthèse de Nadège YAMEOGO

items.title: Sons and Mothers
items.description: Photographs by Amy Elkins 1. When I was 13, not long after my father had committed suicide, I asked my mother, “What’s the Oedipus complex?” “Why?” she replied at once. “Are you afraid you’ve got it?” Maybe. I wasn’t aware of wanting to murder my father, but in the four years after he suffered a massive stroke at 43, he’d been a volatile presence in our house, given to bursts of rage and tears, or rendered ominously mute by his paralysis. When he disappeared on December 6, 1972, leaving my mother, my sister, and me, I was troubled by a sense of profound relief. Unable to understand, let alone forgive, myself, I went searching for insight on the shelves of my parents’ narrow, high-walled study. Books offered a way to replace real self-knowledge with an official version—the idea of “guilt” instead of the intolerable feeling itself. In a volume called Oedipus: Myth and Complex , amid thickets of psychoanalytic jargon, I found what I was looking for. So why did I ask my mother the question, if I already knew the answer? To show off my new command of the term. To set her up for the unreturnable ping-pong smash I must have known was coming at me—to prove I could take it. I shared everything with my mother: Stanford’s football triumphs, the Democratic Party’s defeats, every Little League at-bat, every dream of glory on the stage or page. Why not my Oedipal anxiety? A few days later, she handed me her copy of Sons and Lovers , D. H. Lawrence’s autobiographical novel about a sensitive young man who is shaped and crushed by the love of his domineering mother. “Read this,” she said. “It might help you understand our relationship better.” She was a small-boned, freckled, quick-tempered redhead with ironic blue eyes and astounding energy. She wore her hair short and had no interest in feminine things, or perhaps in being a woman at all. She preferred the company of men, while bitterly resenting their dominance. “I’m somebody’s daughter, I’m somebody’s sister, and I’m somebody’s wife,” she told a Stanford oral historian in 2014 . “Am I somebody?” People said that she spoke in the accent of Birmingham, Alabama, where she grew up in the 1930s and ’40s, but I couldn’t tell. It was just my mother’s voice—gruff, tender, amused, the voice that’s left a hundred indelible maxims in my head: “Ninety percent of tears are self-pity.” “Push down, lick around” (on how to eat an ice-cream cone). “You’re too sensitive and you’re not sensitive enough” (on my character). “There’s no such thing as casual sex.” “Loyalty is my favorite virtue.” “I wasn’t a very good mother, but I was a pretty damn good father.” She loved to spar, and I made an ideal partner: Win or lose, her narcissism was satisfied. She championed me and competed with me—built me up, then knocked me down, then built me up again. At my 50th birthday party, she rose to make what I expected would be affectionate remarks and delivered a scorching roast. I was the recipient of her unending love, her unstinting attention, and her unvarnished judgment. She taught me how to throw a football and swing a bat, shave and tie a tie, and she taught me how to write. I have the scars. For a year or two after my father died, my mother and I went to see a lot of movies together in the art houses of downtown Palo Alto: Chinatown , Scarecrow , Swept Away , Cries and Whispers . This was the early ’70s, before anyone called my hometown “Silicon Valley,” and the movies, in addition to being great, were mortifyingly explicit. Sometimes my mother offered to sit several rows away, which would have made it easier for me to watch the teenage boy in Amarcord fail to satisfy the buxom tobacconist. But my mother was more fragile than ever before or after—some nights I still heard sobbing from her bedroom down the hall—and I always sat next to her, postponing my adolescent rebellion, as it turned out, forever. Except for the black-and-whites of her youth, my mother actually disliked movies, with a contempt that was both aesthetic and moral. Halfway through The Godfather she gave my shoulder a backhand swat: “Aren’t you about ready to leave?” “No, I’m enjoying it.” “ Gratuitous violence. ” Those hours in darkened cinemas following my father’s suicide always puzzled me, until my wife explained: “It was a way for her to be with you and be alone at the same time.” The problem with movies was that they weren’t literature, and literature was the closest thing in our family to religion. My mother’s sect was the short story. Chekhov reigned supreme, followed by Joyce, Faulkner, Flannery O’Connor, Wallace Stegner (my mother’s mentor), and lesser deities. A moralist in a universe without God, she believed that human beings were the alpha and omega of existence, which made her a severe judge of people’s frailties, especially those of people she loved: “Affairs don’t jump at you as you are innocently walking down the road—you have to go in the woods looking for them.” But the writer’s duty is to see the full human truth and tell it as well as possible. In life, a lonely divorcée’s disappointing one-night stand with a sailor half her age whom she met on a plane might have elicited a terse “Pitiful.” But in a short story my mother wrote called “Small Moments,” she gives this character all the ruthless and compassionate understanding of her humanism. She published several small-press collections, the first at age 50: spare, witty, “no fancy dancing,” as if the worst literary sin was self-display. “Frances Benedict’s husband, Emery, was a lawyer. Successful. Frances herself might yet become anything, having tried nothing,” begins a 1967 story called “Early Morning, Lonely Ride.” But every attempt at a novel defeated my mother, and all her life she suffered from writer’s block. Rather than sit in the study at her Underwood manual typewriter, she would weed the backyard, refinish a table, shop for dinner—“Anything not to write, apparently,” she wrote her mother in 1966. A decade later, in a letter to her sister-in-law: “I don’t seem to have much drive to write anymore. I spent the summer trying but I never finished anything. I’d go to bed on, say, Monday night with eight pages of a story, go to bed on Tuesday with only six pages and by Friday I wouldn’t have any.” No one who spent 30 seconds in her presence could imagine that she lacked self-confidence, but inside the ego drive of any writer lurks the threat of falling silent. You believe you’re a singular talent—your parents, your teachers, your ambitions all say so—but the slight chance of finding out that you’re not is unbearable, and part of your vanity is being honest about your own work. All the while, the child in you who craves attention won’t shut up. The whole drama is contained in a few lines my mother wrote me when I was 19, about a story she’d just published: “The story is not much, in fact is kind of a phony. The woman’s motivation needs beefing up but I guess I wasn’t that interested in it. Nonetheless, I’ve gotten a lot of praise—well, not a lot but a couple of spontaneous responses from readers.” The success that my mother desperately wanted as a writer came to her from teaching. She trained several generations of Stanford students in the craft of fiction, including Scott Turow, Tobias Wolff, Michael Cunningham, Jeffrey Eugenides, and Akhil Sharma. She was unsparing but generous with her students. “They’re all human beings, they all have a capacity to grow, and they all have feelings, and never forget those facts,” she told the oral historian. “No matter how silly the story was, there’s always something in it.” She won several awards and retired in the mid-’90s, a sort of local legend . By then the university was becoming the tech juggernaut that it is today, Stanford Inc., squeezing the English department into irrelevance. She lived three more decades as a reminder of another time, a reproachful ghost of humanities past, until her death last year, one month short of 100. I doubt any of my mother’s students bore greater expectations or suffered more under her criticism than her son. I was the only one who could live out her thwarted dreams. 2. Nancy Huddleston was the fifth of five children—born from 1918 to 1925—in a rambunctious, intensely political family. She came into the world battling for attention and prestige. When the dinner conversation ignored her, she threw her bread at a sibling or stood on the table and speechified. In a screwball comedy about her youth, she would have been the wisecracking little sister of the glamorous lead. She wore boys’ clothes and played boys’ sports, started smoking at 13, drinking and joyriding a year or two later. “I was a real happy tomboy,” she once recalled. “I always played with my brothers. My sisters were nonexistent for me.” Her father, George, was a pale, taciturn patriarch who dispensed unquestioned justice to his boisterous clan. In old photographs he is never smiling. He died at age 90, in 1960, a few months before I was born, and I was named for him, but he seemed so ancient that I could never quite believe he was my mother’s father. George Huddleston represented Birmingham in Congress from 1915 to 1937 . He was a populist in the mode of William Jennings Bryan and a racial moderate by the standards of the South, which meant that in the 1920s he denounced the Klan while voting against an anti-lynching bill. Throughout his career Black people were denied the vote in Alabama, allowing him to take radical positions on behalf of Birmingham’s white working class while avoiding the true test of courage in southern politics. He had a diminutive southerner’s resentment of bigness, a political philosophy he called “Jeffersonian,” and he spent his whole career on the losing side—against America’s entry into World War I, against banks and railroads in the ’20s, and against the New Deal, which led to his defeat in 1936. He retired, bought some property, and became a hard-core Dixiecrat. “He sold out all his principles and became very reactionary,” my mother said in 1947, when she was 22 and still living under her father’s roof. When the historian Richard Hofstadter observed that progressivism and reaction can exist together in a certain American political type , usually from the South or West, he might have had my grandfather in mind. [ From the November 1998 issue: Richard Hofstadter’s tradition ] In 1917, at 48, George married his secretary, Bertha, a warm, vivacious woman almost half his age. “Huddlestons don’t gush,” he would insist, and she would retort: “No, they just dry up and blow away.” She escaped from her repressed and repressive husband in bathtub gin and infidelities. He took out an ad repudiating his wife’s debts. She was arrested for driving drunk with one of her lovers, and the incident landed on the front page of several national newspapers. The marriage was “a horror,” their oldest child, my aunt Mary, told me. Amy Elkins for The Atlantic . Source: Courtesy of the Packer family. Huddleston-family photos: Nancy stands at the center of the rear photo, and sits atop a horse in the photo at left. At right, with her father, 1940s. From her father my mother inherited her moralism, dislike of pretension, and sympathy for the underdog. Her mother gave her an enthusiasm for life that allowed her to thrive after tragedy. From the unhappiness of her parents’ marriage my mother acquired a habit of withdrawing into reading and a desire to write. Loyalty being her favorite virtue, she elided all the misery from stories she told about her family. They became comical southern yarns about a squabbling father and mother; a wild but loving tribe of siblings; their Great Dane, Duke, who survived a policeman’s bullet; the legendary incident in the 1936 election when her father, knowing he was going to be defeated, uncharacteristically lost his cool and demolished his opponent’s straw hat with a bottle of Worcestershire sauce. As a child I never questioned this picture. I glamorized the big, raucous Huddleston family, especially after my own turned so grim with my father’s stroke when I was 8. If only there were more of us; if only we had a heroic dog; if only my mother were still a cheerful tomboy instead of a tired, irritable parent; and if only my father fell silent when he was unhappy instead of bursting into tears. It was years before I learned the deeper truth about my mother’s childhood, and I found it in her fiction. Her most moving characters are children, desperate to feel secure in the love of an unreliable mother and remote father. The combative, vulnerable child remained alive in her all her life. At 99 she could still seem like the 3-year-old girl who yanked a pearl necklace off the neck of a family friend who said she was going to vote for Herbert Hoover. My mother came of age in the city that Martin Luther King Jr. called “probably the most thoroughly segregated city in the United States.” Through her teenage years she took Birmingham’s racial order for granted. “I was extremely prejudiced at this time and very conservative,” she later said. “Mrs. Roosevelt, for example, was an abomination on the face of the world.” But when she was 17, in the fall of 1942, something happened that changed her life. [ From the August 1963 issue: Martin Luther King Jr.’s ‘Letter from Birmingham Jail’ ] She had just enrolled at Birmingham-Southern College, a Methodist school that all her siblings had attended. Her two brothers were now in the military, and the campus was nearly empty of male students. One day, one of the few still around (“some thug”) recounted an incident: At a small-town carnival in southern Alabama, a Black boy had grabbed the side of a whites-only merry-go-round and held on until he lost his grip and fell under the spinning platform, which crushed him. A group of white boys, including the narrator, tied the Black boy to a tree and beat him with iron pipes as punishment for crossing the color line, leaving him paralyzed. This incident, and the casual pride of the thug describing his own participation, so shocked my mother that she wrote her first college English paper about it. She began arguing with her sorority sisters over race. Looking for a way to act on her new liberal consciousness, she signed a membership card of a left-wing organization called the Southern Negro Youth Congress. Without telling her parents, she joined a series of clandestine conversations between Black and white students at local colleges. But Birmingham’s racial hierarchy was inescapable, and it insulted the humanity of everyone it touched. When my mother made a point of sitting at the back of the bus on her way to campus, the Black passengers would stand up for the young white lady. Her attitude toward the Black students she met at the interracial dialogues mixed idealization and condescension: She was awed by everything they said, while hoping they wouldn’t make pronunciation errors. In 1947, an Illinois sociologist conducted a study of 50 or so white liberals in Birmingham on the subject of race. Among those interviewed was 22-year-old Nancy Huddleston. Strict confidentiality was promised, but a few years ago my mother’s transcript fell into my hands and exploded. As if self-lacerating honesty could cleanse her racial sins, she eagerly confessed to them all. She said that she had been a conventional racist until 17, “probably to gain my father’s affection,” and an enlightened one after that. Richard Wright was the only Black writer she had read. She had never entered a Black home, and other than servants she knew only three Black people in Birmingham. Her student meetings had smacked of noblesse oblige and accomplished nothing, and she despised her own righteousness. Her liberalism was merely “selfish”—she didn’t want to be deprived of the intellectual and artistic talents of Black people. Her views on race were “acquired attitudes whose urgencies I can ignore at times,” and she had promised not to embarrass her parents by breaking Jim Crow laws. What really got under her skin was the unfairness of “patriarchy,” because it hurt her personally. Her approach to race was sentimental, maybe moral, but not political. That would have demanded real sacrifice. Decades later, I asked what more she could have done. “I could have thrown a bomb, or at least not enjoyed myself quite so much,” she said. “My racial experiences are littered with shame.” In 1945, my mother left Birmingham to study for a master’s in theology at the University of Chicago. She was not even slightly religious, but she wanted to develop her mind, and the only professor at Birmingham-Southern who had taken her seriously (she credited him with saving her from a life of aimless drinking and partying) taught religious studies. Most of all, she wanted to get out of the South. My mother was not a classic beauty, but in Chicago she felt irresistibly attractive. Female-deprived men were coming back from the war, and she could have gone out 10 times a day. She briefly dated a Black man just to prove to herself that her reluctance to get involved with him had to do with his wife and children in Washington, D.C., and not with prejudice: “I would never have tolerated such freshness from any white man.” Her bridge partner and close friend was Morteza Sprague, Ralph Ellison’s literature professor at Tuskegee. Her friendships were intellectual. She studied Reinhold Niebuhr and William James and wrote a thesis on John Dewey. Her time in the university’s more equal and free atmosphere was the happiest of her life. In 1947 she returned to Birmingham with her master’s and stayed a decade. Why did she waste her 20s marooned in her parents’ volatile house, in a rigid and cruel society that she had come to despise and that had no place for a young woman except as a homemaker? She always said that her mother and father needed her, that an unmarried woman was expected to live at home, that back then middle-class white girls didn’t have “careers.” These were conventional excuses, and growing up I didn’t question them. Children don’t see their parents as people with complex, unconscious motives, or as individuals at all. Now I can imagine a story that my mother never told, perhaps not even to herself. It has to do with being a woman and a writer. She would bring armloads of books home from Smith & Hardwick, in downtown Birmingham, and spend her days in her parents’ house reading the great modernists—Kafka, Proust, Mann, Koestler, Hemingway, Faulkner, Wolfe. She began to write autobiographical stories in a sharp, knowing voice. To see the hidden and unlovely truth about everything, especially oneself, with a mid-century-American dose of Freud, was the mark of literary sophistication. She also exchanged flirtatious, barbed letters with several men whom she had met in Chicago. And in both fields, art and love, she was plagued by fear of failure: rejection of her stories, surrender of her independence. If she was attracted to someone, she would turn the affair into a competition for dominance, win, and lose interest, or else find herself succumbing and end it. “Returned from France to receive your thoughtful morsel of intellect and Huddleston voodoo for which I thank you from my heart—but what badinage,” wrote a suitor who signed as “R.” “You know, baby, if you don’t hurry up I’m going to marry somebody else and you won’t have anything but those old books and hair lockets.” R. did marry somebody else, which Nancy learned on the same day in January 1950 that she received her first rejection slip, from this magazine. She had counted on success that winter with either R. or The Atlantic , then decided that she could have both, before coming up with nothing. She wrote to a friend: “Thinking that it was possible for me to have love and creativity, that there could be a both/and, I see that there can also be a neither/nor.” Rejections piled up—hers of the men, the magazines’ of her. Within the confines of the yellow house at 2816 Rhodes Circle, her confidence would soar, crash, rise again. “I’ve gotten six rejections for my hard efforts, have relinquished literature seven times, and have a divine plot for a wonderful story which I hope to start tomorrow,” she wrote to the same friend. “I sharpened my razor at one point, summed up my life as a total failure, and convinced myself there was never such a genius in the long years of civilization.” If she wasn’t a writer, who was she? Her aging father’s last daughter, under his roof and thumb. But if she turned out not to be a genius, she would have to submit to another male authority in the form of a husband who would gradually lose his awe of her and sink into careerism, alcohol, and affairs (this was the 1950s). In Birmingham, where the family name gave her a certain local fame, she could sustain her fantasies without having to test them against life. One persistent and disgruntled beau finally let fly a harsh analysis. “Let’s get on the ball, Nancy, and face a few facts,” he wrote. “You don’t dare admit that you haven’t the courage to face the world, so you take refuge in having to take care of Mummy & Daddy. Because you’re too ‘young’ to accept anything but top-notch success and you’re afraid you don’t have enough of what it takes for that, you withdraw from the world and stay home in your mother’s womb, where it’s a little stifling & quite crowded for one of your size, where you’re not wanted and whence you’ve already been ejected, but where it’s warm, not too uncomfortable, and safe.” He also accused her of being afraid of sex. This was a misguided strategy for conquering such a heavily defended stronghold. I don’t know what happened to the guy, but Nancy didn’t marry him (though she saved his letters). She did see a psychiatrist, but he was unable to solve her other problem: Almost nothing she started got past three pages. The one story she did finish—“ Povera Baby ,” a Hemingway imitation about a spoiled American woman on board an ocean liner to postwar Italy whose infected foot exposes her to the realities of poverty and war—was published in 1953, in Harper’s , no less, alongside an essay by James Baldwin. But success was a curse, and my mother’s struggle to repeat it produced an impasse that lasted the rest of the decade. Writer’s block is different from depression, to which my mother was almost psychologically immune. She had too much energy to sink into torpor—who knew, she might still be a genius. In 1954 her father’s old seat in Congress came open, and she considered running for it, almost as a lark—she was, after all, a woman. Then her older brother George decided that he wanted it. I’m somebody’s daughter, I’m somebody’s sister. My mother snuffed out her own ambition and became the manager and speechwriter of her brother’s winning campaign . Politics was a natural arena for her abilities, and she did some work for the Democratic National Committee. She wasn’t very interested in policy, but she saw ideas in vivid moral colors, she loved a fight, and she had become a passionate Adlai Stevenson liberal. That was how she got to know the man she finally married. In early 1956, on his way to California to start teaching at Stanford Law School, a Jewish lawyer and World War II Navy veteran named Herbert Packer passed through Birmingham to visit a friend, who invited him to a dinner party where another guest was Nancy Huddleston. These two 30-year-olds spent the evening talking about the coming presidential election. For the next two years they exchanged infrequent visits and frequent letters. I never really knew my father. When I was a little boy, before the stroke, he was a kind, overworked, rather distant presence; afterward, he was a person I pitied and feared. But his correspondence with my mother reveals someone unimagined. This is why letters are among the many things whose passing from our lives we will regret. After my mother died, a cardboard box full of them came into my hands, the airmail envelopes covered in stamps and postmarks, and without them I couldn’t tell this story. Letters have a humbling effect on memory. They reveal those closest to us without our distorting presence. They let other people come back to life and have their say. “You are so entirely desirable to me that nothing will ever be the same again for me unless I win you,” my father wrote in 1957, after a visit to Birmingham that left him palpitating. “So it’s my health as well as yours that’s at stake.” Who was this passionate lover? “I am not so moonstruck as to suppose that the doubts of a lifetime can be dissolved in a day. And I know that you will have your bad days, when there is no hope, no belief, just doubt and black despair. But through it all, remember this Nancy: I want you, I need you, I love you.” No wonder she married him—he knew how to talk to her. He pursued, but without coyness or aggression, cards on the table. He gave space and time, but not too much. He understood her resistance and waited it out. This dark, handsome Jew was exotic in Birmingham (her nearly senile father violently opposed him), more than her intellectual equal, but not a man who wanted to dominate her or ever could. He was offering to take her to California, 2,000 miles from the yellow house that had become her prison. By 1958, at 32, marriage might have been now or never. “I went into it with absolute blindness,” she told the Stanford oral historian. “I just knew it was an opportunity to get out and stop being a slug.” So she made what she called, in a letter written a few weeks before the wedding, “the most difficult decision of my life.” In California she was nobody. She had no one to talk with all day except grocery clerks and nothing to do but shop and receive furniture deliveries and wait for her busy, conscientious husband to come back from campus to the apartment in Menlo Park so she could cook dinner or go out with him and his colleagues. Herb volunteered to make breakfast and wash the dishes every Sunday so she could sleep in. Her reading was reduced to cookbooks; she wasn’t writing at all. This was the nightmare of losing herself, and she wondered if she had made a great mistake. And it turned out that she had bound herself to a fragile man. Herb was having trouble finishing a book he’d been contracted to write about the case against Alger Hiss and other American Communists. He was drowning in documents and had lost interest. His writer’s block sent him into a depression that became alarmingly suicidal. When Herb’s new wife returned to Birmingham to see her dying father, his letters, which before the marriage had been so sure, so persuasive, sounded self-pitying and reproachful. On a phone call, he broke down in tears. His inadequacy made him ashamed: He wanted her to need him as much as he needed her. But that would never happen. With his wife’s encouragement and force of will, my father finished Ex-Communist Witnesses . The marriage survived, and two changes allowed my mother to embrace her new life. One day, Herb ran into Wallace Stegner, the novelist and director of Stanford’s highly regarded creative-writing program . Knowing that his wife was sinking into bitterness with her stalled vocation, my father asked if she could take a class. Studying under Stegner, alongside talents such as Ken Kesey, Ernest Gaines, and Wendell Berry, gave my mother the confidence that she could hold her own. Her block lifted; she began to write stories again, and to publish them in quarterly magazines. She felt more like a real writer than ever before. When a rising young star named Philip Roth withdrew his acceptance of a Stanford lectureship, she was asked to fill in and found that she liked teaching more than writing and was better at it. It did not escape her notice that she had ridden into Stanford on her husband’s back. She was somebody’s wife, and she would spend the 1960s in his shadow. One day in 1959, the walls of Stegner’s classroom began to shake. “Don’t worry, Mrs. Packer,” he said. “You’re not having the baby. It’s just an earthquake.” That was the second change: motherhood. 3. My sister, Ann , whom we called Annie, was born in March 1959. I arrived 17 months later. Almost every week for a decade, until my father’s stroke, my mother typed out a long, single-spaced letter on onionskin paper to her widowed mother in Birmingham. The letters create a montage of our California childhoods, sun-drenched scenes shot at close range by a sharp-eyed camerawoman who’s interested in everything about the subject—tedious to most viewers, endlessly engrossing to me. Could you replay that swimming-lesson sequence where I refuse to put my head underwater, then brag to my friends that I dove off the board, only for my mother to expose my lie? Packer-family photos from the 1950s and ’60s, including pictures of the author as a baby and a young boy; his sister, Ann; and his parents, Nancy and Herbert, on their wedding day She was too ambitious and resentful, too masculine, to adore motherhood. She had no use for baby showers, and the thought of breastfeeding disgusted her. She complained about how hard it was to find good babysitting so that she could get her work done (unlike the white ladies of Birmingham, most suburban-California mothers did without help). To put me, and herself, on a better sleep schedule, she gave me phenobarbital and Serpasil, a blood-pressure medication also sometimes used as an antipsychotic. (Apparently these were normal treatments for infant insomnia.) When I came down with a cold in my eighth month, she wrote to her mother: “He can almost sit up, almost crawl, and almost hold his bottle. He is the almost wonder of the world. And if that sounds a little hostile, I guess I have to admit that for the first time since he was circumcised, his having this cold is causing me anxiety and therefore hostility.” But the overwhelming fact of the letters is how much fascinated, puzzled, delighted, annoyed attention she paid to her children. Like every parent she failed us in a thousand ways, some of them barely forgivable, but her attention was a gift, the foundation on which I could grow up without the fear of abandonment that had haunted her as a child. Of course, I was completely unaware of it—that was part of the gift. She spared me the burden of having to become conscious. I was free to live in my own mind, except when she was angry with me, which I found intolerable—then I would do anything to win back her favor. One of my mother’s favorite quotes, usually a dig at someone’s lack of self-awareness, was from Robert Burns: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as others see us!” Can I see myself in her letters? A greedy feeder, cheerful, volatile, wildly curious and easily frustrated, “clinging and adventurous,” indifferent to clothes, unshy because unconcerned with others, so competitive that I have trouble keeping friends? And if this is who I am, how did I get that way? It seems my character was already formed at six months. “Undiscriminatingly friendly, and yet so happy for a little attention”: I admit that sounds familiar. Compared with my hyper-observant sister at the same age, I was noisier, grinnier, and “not as individually aware of people.” All these traits would have consequences. My mother absorbed herself in both her children, but in different ways, with different levels of intensity. She regarded my sister with a sort of objective admiration: so bright and verbal, self-toilet-trained, good at everything she did, “incorrigibly social.” My mother’s investment in me was of another kind: “I must say that I am beginning what promises to be quite a love affair with the little boy.” But a love affair comes with a price, and the letters describe her efforts over the years to shape me after an ideal, constantly adjusting my levels of toughness, sweetness, wildness, self-control. She liked to say that her parents’ generation approached child-rearing as taming savages, her children’s generation saw it as nurturing flowers, and for hers it was like molding clay figures (one of her hobbies). In a letter written in 1968, my mother describes her children’s attitude toward reading. My sister read all the time, a new book every day, simply for the love of it. On the night Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated, Annie said that life in prison wouldn’t be the worst fate for the killer as long as there were books—in fact, she’d sort of like to go to prison and read all day. But my reading came from some internal pressure to know everything about a subject. Over breakfast I read the backs of Cheerios boxes because they displayed capsule biographies of the presidents, and presidential history—especially of the assassinated ones—was one of my obsessions in that year of political violence. My other interest was the NBA, mainly the Los Angeles Lakers. Sports was a passion I would share with my mother for the rest of her life. I barely registered that it left my sister out. “She is doing great in school,” my mother wrote, as if to reassure herself that her commitment to evenhandedness still held, “and has a lot of other interests, cooking and scouts, that aren’t intellectual but are perfectly fine.” Obviously, they weren’t perfectly fine. She found her daughter’s interest in the feminine arts of baking, sewing, clothes, and hair disturbing enough to use an adjective I’ve never heard from anyone else: “Annie is the most fixey child I’ve ever seen.” This was not criticism meant to inspire improvement, because my sister’s fault—being a girl—was irreparable. In turn, Annie disapproved of our mother’s short haircut and slacks. She became a caustic preteen, and a gap opened between them. During the ’60s my father was an important figure at Stanford. Amid the endless cocktail parties and business trips, he was named a top administrator just in time for the anti–Vietnam War protests that nearly destroyed Stanford and other universities. He took the students seriously, which meant that, unlike many of his colleagues, he refused to appease protesters when they occupied an administration building. Force was the opposite of reason, and reason lay at the heart of his philosophy, and his sense of betrayal made him a hard-liner and a lightning rod. He wrote brilliantly in defense of liberal education, but he was not psychologically equipped for a fight like this. My mother shared his values but not his high-mindedness, and she was better suited to do battle: “I wish I had his proxy sometimes, just so I could have some fun socking some people. Not Herb, though. All he wants is what’s generally best.” She was stronger than her husband but much less important, even after she was made assistant professor. Instead of pouring her resentment into her letters, she wrote “Early Morning, Lonely Ride,” perhaps her best story, so tense with marital vitriol that reading it constricts my breathing. Emery, a successful lawyer, and Frances, his restless, unhappy wife, attend a party in San Francisco, where he commands attention and ignores her, provoking her to throw verbal darts his way. When they leave, he insists on taking the wheel even though he’s drunk too much. On Bayshore Freeway they get a flat tire, and Emery is incompetent to change it. A car pulls up with three tough young men inside; it isn’t clear if they intend to offer help or commit rape. Their leader immediately senses the balance of power that favors Frances, and he orders Emery to sit in the back of the car while they change the tire. Frances tells her husband to comply. The leader comes on to her; she angrily rebuffs him. The story ends with Frances at the wheel and her humiliated husband in the back. She imagines how, later, at home, they will console each other by reducing the encounter to an amusing anecdote in which nothing important was at stake. “But for now, as Emery wept silently in the back seat, she drove the car and she was exhilarated.” Jesus! What the hell did my father think when he read this? And yet, around the same time that she wrote “Early Morning, Lonely Ride,” on their eighth anniversary she told her mother, “I believe I could not possibly have done better.” Loyalty, her favorite virtue, made her somebody’s daughter, sister, and wife.
