The author with his father, mother, and sister, late 1960s Our life as a family ended in March 1969 when my mother woke up in the middle of the night to find my father lying beside her stricken by a blocked cerebral artery. She would always blame stress from “the radicals,” but she knew better than anyone that her husband was fragile. In the years that followed he fought valiantly to recover speech and movement, but he had always lived through his rational mind, and it would never be his again. A memory from the early days of the catastrophe: My mother is driving me to the San Francisco airport—I’m flying alone for the first time, to spend a week with a friend’s family in Seattle. At 8 I’m too young to understand that my mother needs some respite and I’m the more exhausting of her children. We’re late, and the airport garage is nearly full. At last she finds a spot and starts to park, when two men in a fancy car sneak in front of her and steal it. My mother, now carrying the entire burden of our wounded family, makes a wide circle around the garage; comes onto a straightaway, at the far end of which the men are getting out of their car; and floors it. As we hurtle toward them their terror looks to be even greater than mine. My mother swerves away in time to avoid committing murder. For a moment she must be exhilarated. She would always say, “When your father got sick …” and this seemed to me an odd phrase. He didn’t have an illness—he was struck down as if someone had given him a blow to the head. In all the years I lived at home, I knew my mother to be sick only once, when I was 5 and a blood clot in her leg turned into deep-vein thrombosis that required her to wear knee-high, flesh-colored compression stockings for the rest of her life. But she didn’t refer to this as her sickness: “I call it an accident, because I don’t like the idea of having an illness.” It was as if getting sick suggested some deeper, probably fatal condition. Better not to get sick at all. Memory needs a story, and the one I tell myself about the period after the stroke—those years when my father grew a silver-flecked black beard because shaving was too hard, and limped along with a cane in his good left hand and a metal brace on his bad right leg, and drove an orange golf cart to campus, and cursed or wept when he couldn’t make himself understood, and my mother was often, in a favorite word of hers, “irritable,” and my sister withdrew further into herself—is a story of unrelieved misery. But my mother’s letters, less frequent than before, less full of energy and humor, tell a different one. They show me plugging away at one obsession after another: presidents and assassinations at 8, basketball and the Greek myths at 9, Stanford football at 10, Little League and World War II at 11, Shakespeare and girls at 12. Memory is notoriously selective, but so are the perceptions that adults have of children. Parents easily miss the secret grievances and torments their children carry inside themselves without the language or license to express them. “The children are in their prime,” my mother wrote a year after the stroke. “They’ve never been dearer, sweeter, more interesting.” She didn’t see any more than I did that the intensity of my interests, and her absorption in them, allowed me to live through the unhappiness of those years without having to experience it. But this left an empty, unformed space where inner resources never developed. So when my father checked into a San Francisco hotel and took an overdose of barbiturates , and when soon after that I decided to be a writer, I was unequipped for either. “I no longer burst into tears when anyone speaks to me of Herb, and in fact was able to sit through the memorial without shedding very many tears,” my mother wrote to my father’s sister in January 1973, eight weeks after his death. “I’m working hard and my friends are loyal and sustaining and the children are always entertaining and occupying, sometimes in ways I’d as soon avoid, but all in all I am being drawn back into life.” Her attachment to life: That’s what saved her. At 32, she had escaped her father’s old Birmingham house and released her energy in writing, teaching, and raising children. Our new California house had filled with cocktail parties for 30 and dinners for 15. Then, with my father’s paralysis, it became empty and silent; my mother stopped writing. His death when they were both just 47 ended her life as an adjunct to men. She never remarried, or even dated much, refusing to compromise the independence that had come to her through loss. She raised two teenagers by herself, got dinner on the table every night, published her first collection, transformed Stanford’s freshman-English program, became a legendary teacher, filled our house with her students and colleagues, and walked our dog, Frank, twice a day. I was too busy being a self-absorbed teenager to understand that, no longer somebody’s daughter, sister, or wife, she was now somebody’s mother—somebody she could shape to her will. Shortly after my father’s death, I took a seventh-grade typing class. The practice of touch-typing got into my head in a way that we would now call obsessive-compulsive: I acquired a mental habit of moving imaginary fingers over imaginary keys, typing out my thoughts as I thought them and my words as I spoke them, which made me conscious of what I was thinking or saying in an almost physically distressing way. Around the same time, I began systematically reading through the titles listed on the back of a CliffsNotes guide to Hamlet , checking them off one at a time, as if CliffsNotes was the ultimate authority on what a writer should read. I tried to sum up each book’s theme in a single sentence, which allowed me to resolve some inner tension caused by all the ambiguities of literary experience and move on to the next title. When the theme eluded me—this happened with Sherwood Anderson’s Winesburg, Ohio —I could reduce myself to tears. I can see now that the compulsive touch-typing and overwrought checking-off of titles were evidence of an anguish whose deeper source eluded me. At the time, all I knew was that I wanted to be a writer and that wanting to be a writer hurt. I showed my mother everything I wrote. The verdict was always good but not good enough , leaving me in agonies of frustration. My adolescent literary efforts are covered with commentary that might as well have been scribbled in my blood. It never occurred to me that my mother’s opinion was that of just one very overinvolved reader; however much it upset me, what she said was Truth. She would hunt down every labored metaphor and mark wherever a story inadvertently shifted point of view (a careless sin). She returned a maudlin stab at Romantic poetry with this observation: “Don’t try to write like Keats. I want you to try to write like Eliot.” Another forehand winner. Eyes burning, I said that I’d write the way I wanted to write—as if being my mother’s prize project didn’t make that impossible. Writing was far from the whole of our relationship. We watched hundreds of hours of TV sports; talked endlessly about politics; bickered over grades (“Why an A–?”), chores, and late nights out. On trivial matters I stood up for myself, and on important ones I thought I was living a life of my own making. In the same way that I couldn’t hear her southern accent or question her criticism, I never associated my desire to be a writer with my mother’s vocation. An idea of greatness that at 9 meant an NBA career like Jerry West’s, and at 12 had me performing onstage like Laurence Olivier, inspired me at 15 and 16 to write like Dickens, then Fitzgerald, then Joyce, then Faulkner. The results were predictably absurd. My mother liked to quote a piece of literary advice from Henry James: “Try to be one of the people on whom nothing is lost!” Unfortunately, I was one of the people on whom a lot of things were lost, including myself. (I was too sensitive and not sensitive enough.) Nor did I follow James’s other famous advice—to write from experience. One of my characters was a British schoolboy who was looking forward to “Michaelmas,” a word whose meaning I didn’t know but I probably borrowed from Dickens. My imagination didn’t brim over with stories. I wasn’t a stylistic prodigy. I had nothing urgent to say. Everything I wrote, even journal entries and weekly letters home from college, carried a grating note of falseness. The words were meant to be overheard and admired. I published stories and poems in my high-school literary magazine because I was the editor, but in college I ran into failure after failure. A classmate in a fiction-writing course wondered why I wrote such formal, convoluted sentences—was I trying to sound like James? Everyone else was trying to sound like Raymond Carver and Ann Beattie, who, in the instructor’s opinion, were more appropriate models. In his office I tried to wheedle an assurance that I was one of the students who would make it. The instructor was crushingly noncommittal. I was doing well at just about everything I tried, except for the thing that mattered most. Amy Elkins for The Atlantic . Source: Courtesy of the Packer family. The short-story collection published by the author’s mother in 1976 was spare, witty, with “no fancy dancing,” as if the worst literary sin was self-display. My sister was a year ahead of me at the same college. One day, when she was a senior and I was a junior, she informed me that she had won a fiction-writing prize. The news surprised us both. She was the one who read to read, not to write. Growing up around writers had made her want to be anything else, because they all seemed unhappy. Our mother was so destroyed by rejection that she never sent her stories to The New Yorker , only small magazines— The Kenyon Review , Southwest Review . This was the sort of detail that my sister, on whom nothing was lost, noticed and I, distracted by my own performances, did not. My sister’s story was based on an episode I knew well. Her best friend in junior high, a brilliant and charismatic girl, had fallen in with an older scene of boys and drugs, shattering her parents. “Jessica at Fourteen” appeared in the campus literary magazine that had rejected every story I submitted. Reading it, seeing the way my sister transformed experience with imagination, the story told from the first-person viewpoint of the girl’s father, the work done through details, the lack of straining for meaning, even the simplicity of the title: I knew that this was what fiction should be. All those years of reading and watching in our mother’s shadow and mine had made my sister the real writer, later a celebrated novelist . She had become what I was supposed to be. My apprenticeship had given me an arduous training in prose style and left a hollow space where a writing self failed to emerge—until, out of college and living in a West African village 8,000 miles from my mother, I was visited by unfinished business from the past. 4. In the summer of 1982 I went to Togo as a Peace Corps volunteer because I didn’t know what else to do. I was vaguely aware that being an undiscriminatingly friendly boy who was happy for a little attention had led me into a dead end, and that I was due for a reckoning. If I wasn’t a writer, who was I? I couldn’t have said this at the time, but I was afraid that the hollow space would become the whole of me. To avoid that, I wanted to put myself through something new and hard. In another time or from a different background, I might have joined the Army. My mother was troubled. Perhaps she knew that the person from whom I needed so much time and distance was herself. Our last days together before I went away for two years were tense, more so because my college girlfriend joined me for a few of them. “I’m sorry I was a bitch so much of the time you were home,” my mother wrote after I was gone, in the first of dozens of letters she sent, each taking three or four weeks to arrive at the local post office. She had been “an, at best, intermittently difficult hostess who is obviously jealous of her son. I think that usually I would control my feelings better.” She did not want to alienate me or separate me from happiness, “even when it doesn’t involve me.” She assured me that I was doing something important and right. As a going-away present, my girlfriend had given me a gold Cross pen. I planned on using it to fill letters and notebooks, to make the strangeness around me meaningful. I might have given up the ambition to be a writer, but I still felt an impulse to write. During my first week in Africa, I lost the pen. Its disappearance was a bad omen that rattled me, as if one of the strands connecting me to my past had been broken, and I might never make it back. In those first days, during training with other volunteers and Togolese English teachers in a small village up-country, a change came over me. It affected my body first: lightheadedness, a dry mouth, a suddenly racing pulse that I started monitoring with two fingertips on my wrist. I should have known that anxiety and even suicidal thoughts are among the potential side effects of chloroquine, the antimalarial medication we had to take. But I had no concept of them; I had never experienced real psychological trouble. The son of a suicide, I didn’t know what depression meant. Instead of locating what was happening to me in neurochemistry, which would have at least provided some rational comfort, I associated it with a change in the outside world. The crowing of roosters in the midday heat; the doughy texture of pounded yams; the children chanting “ Yovo, yovo, bonsoir! Ça va bien? Merci ! ” whenever they saw an American—these were normal features of village life, but in bad moments I experienced them as not just strange but sinister. And I already knew that nothing would ever be the same, even if I went home, because this change that had begun in my head extended beyond the village to the whole universe. I looked at the humid sky and saw only emptiness. Whatever once gave meaning to being alive had drained away, and the loss brought panic. With such long intervals between letters, I tried to keep mine indirect to protect my mother, and perhaps to conceal my weakness from her. But desperation rid my words of the old falseness, and the letters must have alarmed her. “Sometimes when I think how out of touch we are, I feel that I can’t breathe and then I know I can,” she wrote. “Two years is a long time and you are right not to want to view it as an endurance test. If it is that, then you shouldn’t stay. I mean that.” She hardly knew how much trouble I was in, because I kept my darkest thoughts from her. I turned to a practice that had almost always worked in the past and tried to read my way back—to master chaos and fill emptiness with literature. Just as Sons and Lovers was supposed to help me understand my relationship with my mother, I asked her to send books to Africa that I hoped would explain the sudden vacuum of meaning: Kierkegaard on faith and despair, Mann on illness and love , Jung on the shadow, Conrad on the heart’s darkness. In my free time I searched for answers by kerosene lamplight under my mosquito net, taking feverish notes in the schoolboy copybooks I had bought for my lesson plans. All this effort made no difference; reading changed nothing. Instead, it mastered me, as if an insulating layer of intellect had been stripped away and for the first time in my life I was reading undefended, raw. A single sentence had the power to terrify me. [ From the December 2024 issue: George Packer on how ‘The Magic Mountain’ saved his life ] Once, on an hours-long bush-taxi ride north to Togo’s sandstone plateau, I came to a passage in Moby-Dick about the whiteness of the whale: “By its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation,” Melville writes. “Pondering all this, the palsied universe lies before us a leper.” My fellow passengers might not have noticed the American dissolving in front of them as he closed his book and put it away. Amy Elkins for The Atlantic . Source: Courtesy of the Packer family. The author during his Peace Corps stint in Togo, 1983 I found myself thinking of my father. Thinking is too rational: His ghost had taken up residence on my side of the cinder-block, iron-roofed dwelling I shared with a Togolese family of eight. I wanted him to speak to me, but he couldn’t. For the first time in my life I felt close to him, sorrowful for his suffering, wishing I could bring him back from where he had gone, and frightened that I would join him there. I had believed myself untouched by his darkness. Now it was all around me and within me. “I hadn’t realized how closely you had identified with him and how much to heart you would take the knowledge that he had serious problems, and had known despair,” my mother wrote me. “It’s good for you to know that, I think, I hope. And perhaps it is good for you to work through the identification and get to the great difference. But it’s painful, treacherous, overwhelming. And of course trying to understand all that—all the anger you felt, all the love, all the loss—in such difficult physical circumstances and without anyone to help you is really dreadful. Dread. Is that a Kierkegaardian word?” I had always been an achiever among people who loved and admired me, she wrote. Now that I couldn’t be who I really was, “it was almost inevitable that you would begin to unravel a little.” Self-knowledge would set me free, but please go easy. With all of her intelligence and love, and none of her vanity, my mother tried to save me. But I had put myself in a place where only I could do it. I forgot the heartless voids and immensities of the universe long enough to spend hours after class sitting and talking with villagers, in their limited French and my minimal Ewe. The old chief, whose memory went back to the German colonizers before the First World War, told me the history of the village. I recorded his words and the words of others on the Sony Walkman I’d brought to Togo so I could listen to the Police and Bob Marley. I found that I had a knack for talking with people with whom I had almost nothing in common. These sessions provided an escape from myself that completely absorbed me while they lasted, but they had no clear purpose. They gave me nothing I recognized as subject matter for writing. I was hardly using the Olympia manual typewriter I’d brought to Togo; my literary efforts had come to an end. I didn’t know until much later what my life in the village had to do with being a writer—the kind of writer I would become. At the start of my second year, my mother came for a visit. She charmed the children next door with gifts of toy trucks and Winnie-the-Pooh View-Masters, ate pounded yams in pepper sauce with her fingers, and learned a few words of Ewe from the market women. But the life here disturbed her: the torpid afternoons, the evenings without electric light, the sense of stagnation. She advised me to buy more candles and fill my free time with projects. “The people are so kind and hospitable,” she said. “But don’t the Togolese want to make their lives better?” Her readiness at almost 60 to stay in the village should have made me proud, but her company exasperated me. We argued about abstractions like underdevelopment and cultural differences because I couldn’t articulate the real trouble. Her presence was splitting me into two selves: the son she had done so much to create—loving, confident, at ease in the world—and the lost soul with a racing pulse. At the end of the week, I accompanied her down to Togo’s capital for her flight home. When I got back to the village, my brain was swimming and a lump seemed to have formed at the base of my skull. I spent an hour studying the Peace Corps medical guide, Where There Is No Doctor . By nightfall I was so sure that an occlusion in my carotid artery was about to cause a stroke that I asked a bewildered neighbor to drive me to the provincial hospital, half an hour away. In the car I waited for the paralyzing blow to fall, while the mother of the family next door held my hand and tried to reassure me. I was kept overnight and woke up feeling better. The German doctor on duty asked a few questions, barely suppressing his irony, then discharged me with advice to have a drink in a nice hotel from time to time, a packet of anti-anxiety pills, and a piece of paper that said: “Beg. nervous breakdown.” This blunt diagnosis shouldn’t have come as a shock, but until that moment I hadn’t understood my trouble in personal terms—that it might have something to do with my relationship with my mother. In her letter replying to my account of the misadventure, she wrote: “Dear George, please try to be easier on yourself, a better friend than you have been. Don’t be ashamed of limiting the demons, of avoiding them if possible. Don’t be ashamed of finding some new purposes there so that you will be able to achieve/perform/be comfortable with yourself.” What else could a frightened mother say? You’re not your father—don’t do what he did. But this pleading to go back to who I was before seemed dangerous. Anyway, it was too late. At Christmas I traveled through Burkina Faso to Europe for a short visit. In Barcelona everything went wrong. The faces in the Museu Picasso were so grotesque that I could hardly look at them. The girl I had come to see didn’t know what to say to me. One day, I resisted an impulse to jump in front of a city bus and realized that, if I went back to the village for my last six months, I probably wouldn’t make it. For a year and a half I had been barely hanging on. In an English-language bookstore, looking for something to read on the plane back to the States, almost at random I bought a Penguin edition of Orwell’s Homage to Catalonia . The cover image showed a bolt-action rifle with brass cartridges, a crumpled red flag, and an old Spanish newspaper. I knew nothing of the Spanish Civil War, and I knew Orwell only as the author of 1984 , a book assigned in high school. I hadn’t read any of his essays, or any writing of that kind at all. I had never thought of nonfiction the way I thought of novels and poems—as literature. Crossing the Atlantic I was overcome with a sense of utter failure. By leaving early, I had failed my students and friends in the village; and everyone back home, above all my mother; and most painfully I had failed myself. Disgrace and defeat were written on my face, and I avoided eye contact with other passengers. I felt that at 23 I would have to start over, with no idea how. I opened my book and began to read: “In the Lenin Barracks in Barcelona, the day before I joined the militia, I saw an Italian militiaman standing in front of the officers’ table.” Something about this sentence struck me: its lack of fuss, its plainness and strength, the way “I” led quickly and easily to a scene, a view of the world. As I read more, the book started to give me courage. This might be a way of going on: by facing the truth and getting it all down, simply and clearly. First I had to face my mother. In the house where she had raised me, full of the books that had made me want to be a writer, we mostly avoided the subject of why I was home early. Instead, at dinner that first night, we got into an argument about literature. We were talking about Heart of Darkness , one of the books in which I’d searched for answers by kerosene lamplight. My mother thought that the narrator, Marlow, was kept sane by his devotion to work and duty—by repression. To me, Marlow could avoid Kurtz’s fate only by immersing himself in Kurtz’s madness. Of course, we were talking about why I was home early, and what it meant for me, for us. My mother spoke gently, with none of the old sparring, because she knew that she stood to lose something precious. I argued with growing fury, as if not just a literary disagreement but my whole life was at stake. Forty-one years later, as my mother lay dying in the same Stanford hospital where I’d been born, she emerged from dementia long enough to squeeze my hand and tell me: “I love you. I’m proud of you. Now go on about your business.” But that night in January 1984 she was still trying to hold on to the boy she had made. At last, as if admitting defeat, she said: “I thought you were steel tempered in fire.” That was the last time we spent more than a few days together. I went to Boston, for no good reason, and found a job on a construction crew. In the evenings after work, I sat at the Olympia manual typewriter that had gone silent in Africa and started to write. I wrote about the village, and I wrote about my father. This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Sons and Mothers.”

items.title: ‘Feminism Is the Consequence of the “Man Problem,” Not Its Cause’
items.description: The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote A virulent form of misogyny has become the single most important force holding together the American right, Helen Lewis argued in the June issue . Helen Lewis’s “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote” is the most important thing I have read this year. My husband has said that Kamala Harris lost the 2024 election because of the misogyny that exists in America; Lewis’s article proved him correct, with just a teaspoon of humor mixed into an otherwise very frightening topic. Amy Crist Gettysburg, Pa. Upon finishing “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote,” I found myself equal parts stunned and galvanized. Lewis has an extraordinary ability to illuminate what so many of us feel but struggle to articulate, and this article was no exception. The MAGA movement contends that feminism is to blame for American decline. But feminism didn’t emerge from nothing. Feminism is the consequence of the “man problem” Lewis identifies, not its cause. The Bible passage that anti-feminist commentators love to cite is from Ephesians: “Wives, submit to your husbands.” But that’s where they stop reading. The verse goes on to say that a husband must provide for his wife, and love her as he loves his own body. This is not a “do as I say or else” arrangement; it is a covenant of mutual care—her health and happiness are meant to be as important to him as his own, and vice versa. When men forget the instruction to care for their wives as they care for themselves, women have no choice but to learn to care for themselves. I was recently at the pharmacy, and the man ahead of me—trying to pick up a prescription for his sick wife—answered the pharmacist’s questions with “I don’t know; my wife takes care of that.” When a husband utters, “My wife takes care of that,” the word that means “everything.” It means knowing the passwords, the medications and dosages, the appointment schedules. It means knowing what to say to assuage a teenager’s broken heart, whom to call at the school, how to manage a crisis. It means caring for sick husbands and aging parents—sacrificing for the people you love. I am the breadwinner in my family. My husband stayed home and raised our three daughters. The plan was for him to return to work once the girls were in elementary school. But we all know what happens when we make plans—God laughs. My husband now lives with a neurological condition that complicates our lives in ways neither of us anticipated. Does working to provide health care for my children and husband make me less of a woman? Would my husband be mocked in the manosphere for not working? Is staying home to raise children noble only when a woman does it? Erika Jackson Gilbert, Ariz. I worry that “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote” misses a crucial component of the rise of masculinism. I stand in vocal opposition to misogyny and the idiocy of the far-right masculine media sphere. I teach my daughters that they control their bodies and that they should never miss a vote. But I do think that a large cohort of men is struggling with issues that have been ignored, or sometimes even mocked, by the mainstream media. Many men try to be good husbands and parents, only to hear mantras like “We don’t need men” and “There are no good men out there”; on social media, people discuss whether they’d prefer to be trapped in the woods with a man or a bear. Meanwhile, American men are nearly four times more likely than women to die by suicide. The manosphere discusses that issue frequently, as Lewis notes; the mainstream media do not. When men hear negative messages about being a man from the mainstream media but see the manosphere addressing their struggles, they will gravitate toward it. I hope society can learn to address male issues without mocking them. Otherwise, I fear, the extremism will continue. Ben Rodriguez Suffield, Conn. A significant number of men are never fully socialized. These men have few if any friends—and certainly no female friends. Deep down, they may not hate or fear women; they just don’t know how to interact with them. They never learned how to work with or cooperate with them. If one accepts that, then quixotic attempts to repeal women’s suffrage or strip women of social and political freedoms should not surprise anyone. Virgil Jose Apple Valley, Calif. Helen Lewis makes a convincing argument that the noisy, often lewd misogyny of the MAGA right is no longer fringe and presents a real danger to women. This sexist worldview reflects and interacts with patriarchal systems across the world. Examining more than 350 variables across 176 nations, the scholars Valerie M. Hudson, Donna Lee Bowen, and Perpetua Lynne Nielsen have demonstrated that “the fate of nations is tied to the status of women.” Their 2020 book, The First Political Order: How Sex Shapes Governance and National Security Worldwide , shows that nations that subordinate women tend to be more fragile, autocratic, corrupt, and impoverished. The subordination of women appears to produce the kind of governance that leads to worse outcomes for everyone. The sexual political order is, as they write, the “first political order”—what starts in a family shapes a broader community’s politics. Eleanor H. Klauminzer Olalla, Wash. Helen Lewis replies: As you might imagine, this article prompted a large and varied mailbag. I heard from grandfathers—happily married for decades—who couldn’t understand how society seemed to have gone backwards, from middle-aged men who felt overlooked because their problems weren’t fashionable, and from parents who worried about what their sons were watching online. I came away thinking that screen-time limits are good, that schools should do more to accommodate rambunctious boys as well as conscientious girls, and that the Democrats need to develop their own, positive visions of masculinity to compete with those of Andrew Tate and Nick Fuentes. Some of the likely 2028 presidential contenders have started to do that: Gavin Newsom talks regularly about men’s problems, and signed an executive order aimed at improving mental-health services and reducing male suicide rates in California. Pete Buttigieg has learned how to bro out on podcasts such as Andrew Schulz’s Flagrant —the kind of spaces where Donald Trump did so well during the 2024 campaign. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez waded into the debate over the looks-maxxer Clavicular (the guy who claims to have achieved a better jawline by hitting himself with hammers) by highlighting the pressures on young men to conform to unrealistic beauty standards. The conversation is definitely shifting. Behind the Cover In this month’s cover story, “ Empire of Grift ,” Anne Applebaum examines how hardened ideologues and opportunistic profiteers are bending American diplomacy to advance an antidemocratic agenda—and their own financial interests. For our cover, the illustrator Ben Hickey created an ominous image of figures in shadow arrayed around a map of the world, evoking the war-room scenes from Stanley Kubrick’s 1964 film, Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb . Corrections “ The Great Romance Slump ” (September) stated that birth control was legalized for married couples in 1965. In fact, in 1965 the Supreme Court held that the government couldn’t restrict a married couple’s access to birth control. “ Confessions of a Token Black Professor ” (September) described a sign affixed to the wall of a former mill in Lewiston, Maine, as neon. In fact, it is a marquee sign. This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “The Commons.”

items.title: What Comes After America
items.description: Emily St. John Mandel writes science fiction, with the accent firmly on fiction . Imagination, not technical verisimilitude, is her strength; she wisely disregards the scientific in favor of the human. Her indifference to plausibility is a measure of her confidence as a storyteller, and helps snare readers like me, who have a mild allergic reaction to postapocalyptic settings and outer-space odysseys. Her previous novel featured time travel, interplanetary travel, and a cosmic glitch; now, in her challenging new novel, Exit Party , we have accidental teleportation between parallel universes. The underlying theme, though, is irresistible: how shockingly little humanity understands about the sudden swerves and reversals that shape a life—or end it. The new book also offers a prescient invitation to consider the human toll that a world of chaos or repression can exact. Exit Party ’s stunning first sentence leaps ahead to 2031 and peeks into a woman’s soul: “In the first spring after the collapse of the United States, the blossoming of the jacaranda trees felt to Ari like grace.” Newly released after 18 years in prison, 48-year-old Ari Waker is just getting used to a Los Angeles that has seen vicious internecine violence. Although international peacekeeping troops have been withdrawn and the city’s curfew has been lifted, nothing like normalcy prevails. Ari walks with her roommate from their apartment in Echo Park (note the locale) to a party in Silver Lake. There, the incomprehensible happens: Two people from a parallel world materialize at the party, and another person (the host) is teleported in the opposite direction—all by accident. The inexplicable appearances and disappearances are as disorienting for the reader as they are for Ari, who wonders whether she has a brain tumor or is having a stroke. For the three teleported individuals, the experience is a disaster: instant, complete, and irreversible dislocation. In the alternate universe, we soon learn, the “United State” has become a fortress, “closed like a fist,” where the national doctrine is “Harmony at any cost.” There we encounter, among other characters, Ibari, an enforcer of the brutally repressive social order. Abrupt cataclysm is a signature of Mandel’s recent work. Before Exit Party came Sea of Tranquility (2022), The Glass Hotel (2020), and Station Eleven (2014)—all of them ingeniously splintered narratives involving many protagonists, zigzagging timelines, and some kind of shattering event. It’s never clear until the end that the shards of narrative can be assembled to form a coherent story. The big picture that at last emerges in Exit Party features paired life stories of doppelgängers, genetically identical sets of characters who have made decisions in their divergent worlds that move them along radically different paths. Ari and Ibari are the principal “twins.” Though at first they seem utterly dissimilar, they are, as Ibari recognizes late in the novel, “two sides of the same coin.” [ From the March 2020 issue: Ruth Franklin on Emily St. John Mandel’s ‘Station Eleven’ and ‘The Glass Hotel’ ] Repeatedly drawn to criminality (which she associates with freedom), Ari has had more than her share of “hinge moments,” the term she prefers for dramatic, world- and life-changing twists. She launched one criminal enterprise—selling luxury goods bought with stolen credit-card numbers—as a teenager, while living in Brooklyn with an aunt and uncle who dealt in stolen antiques. Soon enough, helped out by her cousin, she was selling U.S. passports. When the Russian Mafia lured her into smuggling people, her cousin, beset by moral qualms, balked. So she hired an assassin to kill him. That’s how she landed in prison. Sprung from jail and hoping to find her footing, Ari drifts instead. She works as a dishwasher and in warehouses, and then becomes, in dizzying succession, a gunrunner, a trophy wife, a philanthropist, an art collector. Arriving in Paris in a car with bulletproof windows (another hinge moment), she wonders, “How many completely separate lives am I going to get to live before I run out of chances.” Mandel makes this resilient character—a serial transgressor with a pragmatic code of ethics, uncannily accurate premonitions, and a touching capacity for regret—sympathetic and compelling. Her last name, Waker, is a clue to her essence: She’s awake, aware. She will always notice the jacarandas. A meticulous observer by profession, Ibari is 79 when we meet her, and has risen to a high rank in the Internal Security Service. She’s as frank about her complicity in the disappearance of rule-breaking fellow citizens as Ari is about her weakness for criminality. Ibari has nonetheless imagined a scenario in which, instead of running surveillance operations for the State, she became a criminal; like her twin, she felt there would be “freedom in that.” The door that swings open at the party remains thereafter obdurately shut. Appalled, puzzled, fascinated, Ari and Ibari (in their parallel worlds) try their best to comprehend what has happened. They investigate, quizzing the accidentally teleported. Eventually, they (and the befuddled reader) learn enough about each other and the different worlds they inhabit to have some thoughts about “entanglement”—about how doubles in their respective universes intersect. Which they do, eerily. Even before she knows anything about Ibari and her career in the secret police, Ari wonders why she herself hadn’t “just become a detective, instead of turning to crime.” She can see the appeal of a life played out in the ranks of the NYPD. She yearns for a homeland where she would be spared the “permanent unease” of encroaching anarchy, where armed fighters aren’t forever shooting at one another on the edge of town. In Exit Party , those who diverge nearly converge, and every echo resonates. When they were young girls, Ari and Ibari each read the same children’s detective novel and both latched on to the same sentence: “True diligence means following the improbable path.” While in prison, Ari had TRUE DILIGENCE tattooed on her left wrist; to judge from the improbable path that Ari and Ibari’s creator has followed, it’s Mandel’s motto too. After growing up in western Canada, mostly homeschooled, Mandel graduated in 2000 from the School of Toronto Dance Theatre. Nine years later, at 30, having abandoned her dream of dancing professionally, she published her debut novel. Like her next two books, it was a noir thriller; all three slipped by more or less unnoticed. Her fourth, Station Eleven , about a flu pandemic “that exploded like a neutron bomb over the surface of the earth,” killing almost every human, won prizes and much-deserved critical praise, and sold remarkably well—before getting a big bump six years later during COVID. Sales of the book passed the 1 million mark shortly after the first episode of an HBO adaptation aired, in late 2021. Station Eleven was Mandel’s own hinge moment. In addition to introducing what has since become her fiction’s hallmark fracturing of time and lives, the novel displayed her calm authority and her easy way with ambitious imaginative gambits—one world erased, another fighting to be born—carried off with barely a trace of writerly flourish: “The caravans had once been pickup trucks, but now they were pulled by teams of horses on wheels of steel and wood.” In Mandel’s work, unadorned realism is at the service of baroque invention, and everything, including the prose, is subordinate to the story. Like all the best stories, hers are character-driven. In Station Eleven , Kirsten Raymonde, a child actor before the pandemic and afterward a skilled warrior, is canny and resourceful in the face of catastrophe. Eight years old when her familiar world ended, and a semi-feral teenager when she hooked up with a ragtag troupe that stages Shakespeare plays and orchestral concerts, Kirsten is permanently traumatized, ferocious when necessary, and somehow still capable of tenderness. She’s a sturdy hook for the reader. Mandel holds tight to some of her characters: She teleports a few between the parallel worlds of her novels. Ari made her debut in The Singer’s Gun (2010), where she was already mercilessly pragmatic and minimally sentimental. An important prop in the new novel is a painting by a minor but vivid character in The Glass Hotel , Lucas Alkaitis, a heroin-addicted artist, talented and doomed, “on the run from mediocrity and Brylcreem and grey flannel suits.” Lucas himself also reappears, still an addict, still committed to his art, in a curious coda to Exit Party set in his Manhattan studio in 1960—a final, wrenching narrative swerve. In Sea of Tranquility , you’ll find a Mandel stand-in: a newly famous writer in the year 2203 who has left her moon-colony home for planet Earth to embark on a globe-spanning book tour. Separated from her family, she finds herself unmoored, homesick. An interviewer in Estonia asks her what it’s like to have published a tremendously successful book. She answers, “I wrote three books that no one noticed, no distribution beyond the moon colonies, and then … it’s like slipping into a parallel universe.” She continues, “I somehow fell into a bizarre upside-down world where people actually read my work. It’s extraordinary. I hope I never get used to it.” One of the projects of modernism (and postmodernism) is to unsettle our confidence in the coherence of the self and thereby reveal the truth about our disjointed identity, so often sabotaged by an unruly unconscious. The so-called neomodernist novelist Rachel Cusk has declared that she is “not interested in character because I don’t think character exists anymore.” It seems to me that Mandel, who merrily jettisons narrative conventions and plays cunningly with timelines, nonetheless insists on the essential coherence of her fictional creations. How many completely separate lives can Ari live and still track as a character? “I took out a contract on my cousin,” she says to the host of the Silver Lake party. “It was a mistake and I’m not that person anymore.” I don’t believe her. Though she probably would not now pay to have a close relative murdered, she remains the ruthless person who once did. [ Read: Emily St. John Mandel’s writing advice ] All of the doubling that powers the plot of Exit Party prompts us to consider how we recognize ourselves and others—whether we believe in the integrity of our persona and theirs. What is the essential stuff of our identity? What makes us whole? In The Singer’s Gun , Mandel has Anton Waker, the cousin Ari thought she wanted dead, provide an answer: It’s details, “small and personal and utterly beautiful and mundane, that make up the fabric of a person’s life.” Hinge moments may matter less than humdrum daily doings. We change tack, break free, and start over, yet we carry with us the stubborn imprint of all our old habits, the jumbled storehouse of memory, and a long trail of sensory data so familiar that it goes unnoticed. We endure. And we suffer, due to circumstances beyond our control. This is where the doubling of the radically different nations comes in. Which is less awful, the calm and sinister surveillance state that Ibari serves with growing reluctance, or the “fracturing continent” that Ari yearns to escape? At first Ari reacts to chaos with a rueful calm—“You don’t notice the supply chain till it collapses”—but after years of “flashes of gunfire at night” from militia skirmishes that “stopped just short of all-out war,” a bone-crushing weariness sets in. As she knows, “Societal breakdown is exhausting.” The “malevolent weight” of a tyrannical government is similarly sapping. When the secret police is everywhere, Ibari wryly notes, “anyone can be surveilling you at any time, including the person whom you are yourself surveilling.” To live peacefully, you make believe everything’s fine, ignoring “black cars moving too slowly down sunlit streets, unsmiling plainclothes agents in pairs, drones gliding quietly through the air.” At the academy where she trained to join the secret police, Ibari was told, “A harmonious society comes at a price.” The instructor added, “And we are not just the ones who exact that price, we are the ones who pay it.” Mandel declines to identify any specific ideology in either world. No dictator is referred to in the totalitarian regime; no feuding warlords are named in the failed state. In both places, the status quo has evolved without recognizable human agency. That’s simply how it is—for now. Ibari comes to treasure the phrase “ No country lasts forever ,” because “there was such hope in that.” A bitter sort of hope, but one that chimes with the spirit of the novel as it winds down, attuned to fluid time as well as fluid space. With Edna St. Vincent Millay’s “famous little poem” about burning the candle at both ends in mind, the artist Lucas Alkaitis (soon to die of a heroin overdose) reflects, “The point isn’t that the candle won’t last the night. Everything is temporary. The point is that the light is gorgeous while it lasts.” This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “What Comes After America.”

items.title: 2027: Atiku will win 19 states in North, 3 in Southwest — Kenneth Okonkwo
items.description: Kenneth Okonkwo, spokesperson for the Atiku Abubakar presidential campaign has projected that former Vice President will win all 19 states in the northern region and three states in the Southwest in the 2027 presidential election. Okonkwo made the projection during an interview on AIT’s Democracy Today on Monday while assessing the chances of the major contenders ahead of the election. According to him, the African Democratic Congress, ADC, on whose platform Atiku is expected to contest, has already gained sufficient support across the North. “Let me tell you the path to victory for Atiku. The 19 states of the north have fallen for ADC. Settled,” he said. Okonkwo attributed the projected support for the opposition to growing frustration with the economic policies of the President Bola Tinubu administration. He cited the minimum wage and rising petrol prices as examples of the economic pressures facing Nigerians. “This government is irrational from their decisions. They are anti-people, and the people have gotten the message because you’re paying somebody 70,000 as minimum wage, and fuel is almost N1,500,” he said. He added that the economic situation had made it increasingly difficult for workers to meet basic needs. “Your 70,000 can no longer afford you half-tank if your tank is 100 liter without rent, without food,” Okonkwo said. The former Labour Party chieftain also predicted gains for the opposition in the South-South, saying Atiku’s running mate would attract support in the region. “South South, we are going to win in some states, and we’re going to get more than two,” he said. “Then we’re going to get more than 25 percent in all the South-South states because who will not like their own son to be vice president?” Okonkwo further projected that the opposition would win three states in the Southwest, identifying Osun, Ondo and Ogun as likely targets. “In the Southwest, we most likely get three states. We may win Osun. We won Osun last time in 2023,” he said. He also pointed to what he described as crises within the APC in Ondo and Ogun states as factors that could work in favour of the opposition. “Then Ondo, because there are a lot of crises in the APC. Yes, Ogun. There are a lot of crises,” he said. Okonkwo also claimed that Tinubu lacked sufficient popularity in Lagos, the President’s political stronghold. “The Tinubu has never been popular in Lagos,” he added. The post 2027: Atiku will win 19 states in North, 3 in Southwest — Kenneth Okonkwo appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Examination malpractice is rising, not declining – EduWatch
items.description: The Executive Director of Africa Education Watch (Eduwatch), Kofi Asare, has disagreed with claims that examination malpractice is declining, saying available evidence instead points to a significant rise in the problem. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Tuesday, September 15, Mr Asare said the data shows examination malpractice increased from about 0.9% in 2018 to 13.5% in 2024, with the rate rising further to 14.8% in 2025. He said Eduwatch is therefore not convinced by claims that increased arrests of offenders demonstrate a decline in examination malpractice. “I disagree with the President’s assertion that examination malpractice is declining.” According to Mr Asare, the trend between 2024 and 2025 shows that the situation has worsened rather than improved. “Between 2024 and 2025, it did not decline. It will increase further from 13.5 percent to 14.8 percent. We are waiting for 2026 data.” He said the figures do not support the argument that examination malpractice has declined since the current government assumed office. “Since this government resumed office, it has not declined. Going by the trend, it hasn’t declined. It’s already from 13.5 percent to 14.8 percent.” Mr Asare also pointed to data from the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE), saying the level of malpractice associated with subject cancellations and entire results increased sharply between 2024 and 2025. “If you look at BECE, actually, malpractice level, subject cancellations, both entire results and then subject cancellations, actually doubled, more than doubled from 4.22 in 2024 to 28.95 percent in 2025.” He said although a decline was recorded in 2020, the level of malpractice remains higher than the 2024 figure. Mr Asare said Eduwatch views examination malpractice as a behavioural challenge that requires a change in attitude and behaviour rather than an approach focused mainly on arrests. “For us at Eduwatch, we see this as a behavioural challenge for which the solutions should be change in attitude and behaviour.” He explained that Eduwatch measures progress by looking at the prevalence of malpractice rather than the number of people arrested, particularly because comprehensive data on arrests is not available. “We measure progress by the number of people participating in the fraud, not the number of people being arrested, because we don’t have data for that.” Mr Asare said the available evidence shows a worrying long-term trend, with the proportion of examination malpractice rising from about one per cent in 2018 to 13.5 per cent by 2024 and further to 14.8 per cent in 2025. He also raised concerns about the number of candidates affected by subject cancellations, saying more than 7,000 candidates had their results cancelled on the basis of subject-related examination malpractice. He said the figures should prompt education authorities to focus on changing the behaviour and attitudes that encourage examination malpractice. Mr Asare maintained that the 2026 data will be important in determining whether the trend has finally changed, but until then, the available statistics do not support claims that examination malpractice is declining.

items.title: Full List: Stadiums that will host UEFA finals from 2027 to 2029
items.description: UEFA has confirmed the stadiums that will host some of the biggest European football finals between 2027 and 2029. The selected venues span several major football cities across Europe, including Munich, Barcelona, Lyon, Cardiff, Bucharest, Belgrade, Turin, Budapest and Amsterdam. The fixtures cover the UEFA Champions League, UEFA Women’s Champions League, UEFA Europa League, UEFA Conference League and UEFA Super Cup. Here is the full list of stadiums that will host UEFA finals between 2027 and 2029: 1. Munich Football Arena – Munich The Munich Football Arena in Germany will host the 2028 UEFA Champions League final. The stadium, home to Bayern Munich, is one of Europe’s most prominent football venues and will welcome the continent’s biggest club competition in 2028. 2. Camp Nou – Barcelona Barcelona’s iconic Camp Nou has been selected to host the 2029 UEFA Champions League final. The stadium will provide the setting for the decisive match of the Champions League, bringing Europe’s elite clubs to the Catalan capital. 3. Parc Olympique Lyonnais – Lyon-Décines The 2028 UEFA Women’s Champions League final will be played at Parc Olympique Lyonnais in Lyon-Décines, France. The venue will host the showpiece match of Europe’s premier women’s club competition. 4. National Stadium of Wales – Cardiff The National Stadium of Wales in Cardiff will host the 2029 UEFA Women’s Champions League final. The decision means Wales will stage the final of one of European football’s biggest women’s competitions. 5. National Arena – Bucharest Romania’s National Arena in Bucharest has been selected to host the 2028 UEFA Europa League final. The Romanian capital will welcome clubs competing for the Europa League trophy in 2028. 6. National Stadium Serbia – Belgrade The 2029 UEFA Europa League final will take place at the National Stadium Serbia in Belgrade. Serbia will therefore have the opportunity to host the final of one of UEFA’s major men’s club competitions. 7. Juventus Stadium – Turin The Juventus Stadium in Turin, Italy, will stage the 2028 UEFA Conference League final. The home of Juventus will host the competition’s decisive match in 2028. 8. Puskás Aréna – Budapest Budapest’s Puskás Aréna has been chosen as the venue for the 2029 UEFA Conference League final. The Hungarian capital will host the final as the competing teams battle for the European trophy. 9. Johan Cruyff ArenA – Amsterdam The Johan Cruyff ArenA in Amsterdam will host the 2027 UEFA Super Cup. The annual fixture brings together the winners of the UEFA Champions League and UEFA Europa League. 10. Astana Arena – Astana The 2028 UEFA Super Cup will be staged at Astana Arena in Astana, Kazakhstan. The fixture will bring the winners of Europe’s two leading men’s club competitions to Kazakhstan for the Super Cup. The post Full List: Stadiums that will host UEFA finals from 2027 to 2029 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Coopération transfrontalière : Les États de l’AES examinent de nouveaux projets de textes
items.description: Le ministre de l’Administration territoriale et de la Mobilité, Émile Zerbo, représentant le premier ministre Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a présidé, ce mardi 15 septembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, la cérémonie d’ouverture de la rencontre de validation et de signature des projets de textes sur la coopération transfrontalière entre les États membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES). La rencontre se tient du 15 au 16 septembre. Pendant deux jours, les autorités administratives des régions frontalières des États membres de l’AES se réunissent pour échanger sur les mécanismes de renforcement de la coopération transfrontalière. Les travaux visent notamment à favoriser le dialogue entre les autorités des zones frontalières afin de contribuer à la stabilité, à la libre circulation des personnes et des biens, ainsi qu’au développement intégré des espaces frontaliers. Plus de détails à venir sur Minute.bf

items.title: Credit Unions encouraged to use technology to improve service
items.description: Managers of Credit Unions have been advised to utilise technology to provide efficient and accessible services to their members, aiming to expand membership. The President of the Ghana Association of Co-Operative Credit Union Managers, Kennedy Yeboah, who made the call, cautioned against the unpredictable nature of the technological landscape, entreating management to ensure they safeguard their systems against Addressing the 27th Annual and Educational Conference for the association, held in Ho, he expressed optimism that these initiatives would boost the growth of the Unions, urging them to safeguard against fraud, cybersecurity among others. “Our members increasingly expect financial services to be convenient, accessible, secure and available when they need them. The question before us is therefore no longer whether credit unions should embrace digital transformation but how quickly, responsibly and effectively can we do so?” “But digital transformation also introduces new risks. Cybersecurity, data protection, fraud, system resilience and digital literacy must therefore receive the same level of strategic focus as the technology itself.” “I therefore call on credit union leaders to view technology not just as an IT function, but as a crucial strategic business priority,” he said. He also advised managers to concentrate on building credit unions that are “strong, resilient, innovative, member-focused and sustainable” and urged CEOs, boards and managers to work together harmoniously to achieve their goals. Mr Yeboah also emphasised the importance of ongoing human capacity development to equip staff with up-to-date skills needed to navigate the modern financial sector and improve services. “We must continually enhance our knowledge, skills and professional standards. We must keep investing in ourselves and in the next generation of credit union leaders,” he said. The National Board Chairman of the Ghana Co-operative Credit Union Associations, Dr Samuel Otu-Nyarko, encouraged members to adhere to the Bank of Ghana’s regulatory framework and to leverage available opportunities. He acknowledged that compliance may pose challenges but also create opportunities to improve governance, operational resilience, and public confidence. “As your Apex institution, CUA remains committed to engaging constructively with the Bank of Ghana, the Department of Cooperatives and other stakeholders to ensure that the interests of our member credit unions are effectively represented while fostering a regulatory environment that promotes safe, sound and sustainable growth.” “The Board firmly believes that compliance should not be seen as an administrative burden but as an investment in institutional credibility and long-term sustainability,” he stressed. He further indicated that the Board aims to “strengthen governance systems, improve enterprise risk management, promote digital transformation, build institutional capacity, improve financial sustainability, and deepen member confidence in the credit union brand.” “These priorities reflect our commitment to ensuring that CUA remains a strong, responsive and forward-looking Apex institution capable of supporting member credit unions in an increasingly competitive financial landscape,” he added. The Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Credit Unions Association, Cyprian Basing, revealed that the association has about 500 members, serving approximately 2.89 million individuals. He also mentioned that the Ghana Credit Union Movement holds total assets of GH₵8.23 billion, with a loan portfolio of GhC3.50 billion, used for financing businesses, homes, education, agricultural expansion, among other purposes. He called for strategic positioning to consolidate these gains by investing in service enhancement and adopting stringent management and governance policies. “These figures are impressive, but they also place a greater responsibility on us all. As our movement grows in size, it must also strengthen. As our assets increase, our governance must improve. As our membership expands, the quality of our services must also improve.” “As technology transforms financial services, we must ensure that every credit union-large or small—is equipped to compete confidently in the digital era. Growth without innovation will not sustain us. Innovation without discipline will not protect us. And transformation without strong leadership will not endure,” he explained.

items.title: Contribution : Du ventre de l’Atlantique à la plaine de Gandon : le jour où le gaz sénégalais a cessé d’être une promesse (Par Aziz Fall)
items.description: Sur le tarmac de la base militaire de Ouakam, une forte délégation conduite par le ministre de l’Énergie et du Pétrole, Dr El Hadji Abdourahmane Diouf, prit place à bord d’un avion militaire. Cap au nord : Saint-Louis, puis la plaine de Gandon. L’image avait valeur de symbole. C’était l’État lui-même qui se mettait en mouvement, avec ses propres moyens, vers le lieu où allait s’écrire une page de son histoire énergétique. Pour cet ancien étudiant de l’université Gaston-Berger, le voyage avait sans doute aussi un parfum de retour. Sous les ailes, la Grande Côte déroulait son long ruban de sable entre la terre et l’océan. À l’approche de Saint-Louis, quelque part au large, invisible depuis le hublot, reposait la richesse qui avait tant fait parler. Ce vol remontait vers le Nord le chemin que le gaz, un jour, descendra vers Louga, Thiès et Dakar. Au bout de ce voyage, un geste. Il est de ceux qui, sous leur apparente banalité technique, portent le poids d’une histoire : un tube d’acier descendu dans une tranchée, soudé au suivant, recouvert de terre. Rien, à première vue, qui mérite qu’on s’y arrête. Et pourtant. Avec la pose de la première canalisation du Réseau gazier du Sénégal, notre pays vient de franchir une ligne invisible, celle qui sépare la promesse de la réalité. Pendant près d’une décennie, le gaz sénégalais a mené une existence paradoxale. Il était là, sous les eaux de l’Atlantique, attesté par les forages, chiffré en milliards de mètres cubes, et pourtant insaisissable. On en parlait comme d’un trésor de légende : les uns pour promettre l’abondance, les autres pour prophétiser la malédiction. Il a nourri les plateaux de télévision, les tribunes, les meetings et les soupçons. Il est devenu un argument, parfois une arme, rarement un projet commun. Trop souvent, les positions prises à son sujet obéissaient moins au souci de l’intérêt général qu’aux calculs du moment politique. Le gaz était partout dans le débat public, et nulle part dans la vie des Sénégalais. Ce temps-là s’achève. Le gaz n’est plus une idée : il devient un tracé. Quatre-vingt-cinq kilomètres environ. C’est la distance qui sépare le hub de Grand Tortue Ahmeyim de la centrale électrique de Gandon, aux portes de Saint-Louis. Une quarantaine de kilomètres sous la mer, autant sur la terre ferme. Un fil d’acier qui relie le ventre de l’Atlantique à la plaine de Gandon, l’invisible au tangible, la ressource au besoin. À l’extrémité de ce fil, une centrale de 250 mégawatts dont Senelec achètera la production. Et dans cette centrale s’opérera une alchimie décisive : la molécule deviendra électron. Le gaz de nos eaux deviendra la lumière de nos foyers. Pour la première fois, une richesse du sous-sol sénégalais ne prendra pas seulement le chemin des méthaniers et des marchés lointains. Elle remontera vers nous. Car de quoi parle-t-on réellement ? L’électricité n’est pas une commodité parmi d’autres. Elle est la condition de possibilité de presque tout le reste. Pas d’industrie sans elle. Pas de chaîne du froid pour le pêcheur de Guet Ndar, pas de couveuse fiable dans nos maternités, pas de soudure pour l’artisan, pas de révision pour l’étudiant, pas de bloc opératoire qui tienne. Le coût du kilowattheure est le prix d’entrée de toute ambition économique et sociale. Un pays qui produit une électricité chère se condamne à des industries fragiles, à des ménages étranglés et à une souveraineté de façade. Jusqu’ici, nous avons largement brûlé du fioul lourd et du charbon importés, payés en devises, soumis aux humeurs des marchés mondiaux. Leur substituer un gaz extrait de nos propres eaux, c’est rapatrier une part de notre destin énergétique. C’est cesser d’acheter à l’étranger ce que la nature a déposé à nos portes. Il est juste que ce premier segment parte de Saint-Louis, ancienne capitale, ville d’eau et de mémoire. Mais Gandon n’est qu’un commencement. Le réseau a vocation à s’étirer vers Louga, Thiès puis Dakar, pour former une ceinture gazière irriguant centrales et zones industrielles. Ce qui naît aujourd’hui dans une tranchée de la plaine de Gandon, c’est la première vertèbre d’une colonne qui pourrait porter l’économie du pays pour les décennies à venir. Mais ce tube ne s’est pas posé tout seul. Derrière chaque kilomètre de tracé, chaque étude, chaque contrat négocié, il y a des visages. Ceux d’une jeune génération de Sénégalais, ingénieurs, géologues, juristes, financiers, techniciens, spécialistes de l’environnement, qui ont fait de ce projet à la fois une affaire personnelle et une cause nationale. Ils ont grandi dans un pays où l’on disait volontiers que ces choses-là se faisaient ailleurs, par d’autres, pour d’autres. Ils ont refusé ce destin d’éternels spectateurs. Formés ici ou au-delà de nos frontières, ils sont restés ou sont revenus, porteurs d’une conviction simple : le Sénégal peut concevoir, piloter et maîtriser ses propres infrastructures stratégiques. Leur trait commun n’est pas l’âge. C’est le talent, et plus encore l’audace de voir grand. Là où d’autres voyaient dans chaque difficulté une raison de renoncer, montages financiers complexes, négociations face à des multinationales rompues à l’exercice, calendriers bousculés, scepticisme ambiant, procès d’intention, ils ont vu les ingrédients mêmes de l’histoire qu’ils se devaient d’écrire pour leur nation. Car aucune épopée ne s’écrit sans adversité. Les obstacles ne sont pas l’interruption du récit : ils en sont la matière. Il faut le dire, et le dire fort. Dans un débat public trop souvent dominé par le soupçon et le dénigrement, ces femmes et ces hommes ont répondu par le travail. Non par des slogans, mais par des plans, des études d’impact, des nuits blanches et des heures de négociation. Non par des postures, mais par des résultats. Leur réussite dépasse le seul secteur de l’énergie. Elle adresse un message à toute la jeunesse sénégalaise, trop souvent tentée par le découragement ou par l’exil : il est possible de bâtir ici, de peser ici, de laisser une trace ici. Le contenu local n’est plus une ligne dans un texte de loi ; il devient une réalité de chantier. Cette génération a trouvé en Pape Momar Lô, directeur général du Réseau gazier du Sénégal, un capitaine à sa mesure. Il a su construire autour de ce projet une belle narrative, patiente et lucide, qui ne cède ni à l’emphase ni au découragement. Son leadership inspire parce qu’il ne se contente pas d’annoncer : il donne un sens à l’effort, relie chaque étape technique à un horizon national et transforme un chantier en récit collectif. À Gandon, devant les autorités et les partenaires réunis, il a résumé d’une formule l’esprit de son équipe : « Peut-être est-ce justement cette jeunesse qui nous a donné une force particulière : l’audace de croire en cette ambition et surtout la capacité de la transformer en réalité. » Ce leadership s’inscrit dans une continuité qu’il serait injuste d’oublier. Avant lui, Joseph Médou, ingénieur géologue venu de Petrosen, a tenu la barre du RGS de 2022 à 2024. Sous sa direction ont été menés une bonne part des travaux préparatoires : études d’impact, concertations avec les territoires, maturation technique des segments du réseau. Les grands ouvrages sont des courses de relais : celui qui franchit une étape doit beaucoup à ceux qui lui ont transmis le témoin. Par-delà les alternances, l’État continue, et c’est aussi cela que raconte ce premier tube. Ce récit collectif rappelle une vérité que rien ne pourra remettre en question : ce qui est bon et excellent finira toujours par damer le pion à ce qui est médiocre et désolant, malgré l’asymétrie de leur visibilité. Car cette asymétrie est réelle. La critique facile se propage plus vite que l’étude rigoureuse. Le soupçon voyage plus loin que la réalisation. Une rumeur fait le tour du pays en une journée, quand un kilomètre de gazoduc exige des mois de travail silencieux. Mais le bruit s’épuise, et l’ouvrage demeure. Les polémiques passeront ; le gazoduc, lui, restera, à transporter sans bruit la preuve de ce qui était possible. Mais célébrer n’est pas renoncer à la lucidité. Poser un tube n’est pas achever un réseau. Pape Momar Lô l’a lui-même rappelé ce jour-là : « Aujourd’hui, nous ne célébrons donc pas un aboutissement. Nous marquons un commencement. » Les délais ont déjà glissé, les coûts sont considérables, et le chemin reste semé d’étapes à franchir : mise en service de la centrale, fixation d’un prix du gaz domestique réellement avantageux, transparence des contrats, respect de l’environnement et prise en compte des populations riveraines, notamment des communautés de pêcheurs dont l’océan est le seul capital. Le débat public ne doit donc pas s’éteindre, mais changer de nature. Il ne porte plus sur l’existence du gaz, mais sur la manière dont il servira le plus grand nombre. Un débat moins spectaculaire, mais plus utile. Un jour, peut-être, un enfant de Saint-Louis allumera une lampe pour faire ses devoirs sans savoir que la lumière qui l’éclaire a voyagé depuis les profondeurs de l’océan, à travers des kilomètres d’acier imaginés et portés par une génération de Sénégalais qui avait choisi d’oser. Il ne connaîtra ni les polémiques, ni les procès d’intention, ni les années d’attente. Il connaîtra seulement une lumière qui ne s’éteint pas. C’est à cela que sert ce tube. C’est pour cela que ce moment compte. Le gaz sénégalais a cessé d’être une abstraction. À nous, collectivement, de veiller à ce qu’il ne devienne jamais une déception. Aziz Fall, Administrateur du Réseau gazier du Sénégal

items.title: Mali : Sifi Ghrieb annonce une prochaine visite d’Assimi Goïta à Alger
items.description: Le Premier ministre algerien Sifi Ghrieb a effectue le 14 septembre un deplacement officiel au Mali. Celui-ci fait suite au sejour a Alger de son homologue malien, le general Abdoulaye Maïga, le 24 août dernier. Sifi Ghrieb a ete recu a Bamako par le president de la Transition, le general Assimi Goïta, dans un climat qualifie de fraternel par les deux parties. Lors de son intervention, Sifi Ghrieb a transmis au president malien les salutations du president Abdelmadjid Tebboune, ainsi que ses vœux de « croissance et de prosperite » pour le peuple malien, dans la securite et la stabilite. Le Premier ministre algerien a notamment insiste sur le caractere historique des relations entre les deux pays. Il a rappele que leurs liens, consolides durant la lutte commune pour l'independance, reposent sur la fraternite, la solidarite et le bon voisinage. Une prochaine visite d'Assimi Goïta a Alger La principale annonce de cette rencontre concerne toutefois une prochaine visite du president malien en Algerie. Assimi Goïta a accepte l'invitation qui lui a ete adressee par Abdelmadjid Tebboune. Selon Sifi Ghrieb, les preparatifs de ce deplacement sont deja en cours. Il doit permettre de consolider la nouvelle dynamique engagee dans les relations entre Alger et Bamako et de porter la cooperation bilaterale a un niveau correspondant aux aspirations des deux peuples. Cette annonce survient apres la visite a Alger, le 24 août dernier , du Premier ministre malien Abdoulaye Maïga. L'echange de visites de haut niveau traduit, selon Sifi Ghrieb, une volonte politique commune des deux dirigeants de relancer et de renforcer les relations algero-maliennes. Alger et Bamako veulent approfondir leur concertation regionale Les deux responsables ont egalement echange sur les defis auxquels sont confrontes leurs pays et, plus largement, la region du Sahel. Ils ont souligne la necessite d'intensifier la concertation et la coordination regionales afin de faire face a ces enjeux. Alger et Bamako souhaitent notamment s'appuyer sur leurs capacites respectives pour contribuer a la paix, a la securite et au developpement dans la region. Sifi Ghrieb a enfin remercie les autorites et le peuple maliens pour l'accueil reserve a la delegation algerienne. Ce deplacement a Bamako s'inscrit ainsi dans un contexte marque par une multiplication des contacts au plus haut niveau entre les deux pays.

items.title: GBA President calls for reasonable, proportionate bail conditions
items.description: President of the Ghana Bar Association (GBA), Efua Ghartey, has called on investigative and prosecutorial authorities to ensure that bail conditions imposed on suspects are reasonable, proportionate, and consistent with the law. Speaking at the Ghana Bar Association Conference 2026/27 in Ada on Monday, September 14, Mrs Ghartey said such conditions must comply with Article 14 of the 1992 Constitution, which safeguards the rights of persons who have been arrested or detained. Her remarks formed part of discussions at the conference, which was held under the theme, “150 Years of Ghana’s Legal Evolution: Transforming the Profession and Driving its Future with Industry.” Mrs Ghartey stressed that bail conditions should reflect the circumstances of each case and must not be excessive, particularly given the constitutional principle that an accused person is presumed innocent until proven guilty. “Bail conditions imposed by investigative and prosecutorial authorities should always conform to the requirements of Article 14 of the 1992 Constitution and must be reasonable. It must also be proportionate and consistent with the presumption of innocence,” she said. She further proposed the establishment of a Human Rights Watch Committee within the legal profession to monitor compliance with Article 14 and other human rights provisions of the Constitution. According to Mrs Ghartey, such a committee could provide greater assurance to citizens that their rights would be protected when they come into conflict with the law. She said the committee could be particularly useful in cases involving the arrest and detention of social commentators and TikTokers, where questions of due process and access to legal assistance may arise. “It has been suggested that for the proper monitoring of Article 14 and other human rights provisions in the Constitution, a Human Rights Watch Committee ought to be considered to give the citizenry some assurance that in cases, for instance, where social commentators have been arrested, the TikTokers, the committee will be able to give the requisite legal aid to suspects,” she said. She said this would strengthen public confidence in the protection of fundamental human rights and the administration of justice.

items.title: Conakry : un travailleur expatrié tué et plusieurs blessés graves dans un accident de la route à Kagbélén
items.description: Un accident de la circulation s’est produit tôt ce mardi 15 septembre 2026, entre 4 heures et 5 heures du matin, à Kagbélén-Plateau. Le bilan fait état d’un mort, un travailleur expatrié et de cinq blessés graves. Selon les témoignages recueillis sur place, l’accident a impliqué un camion immatriculé AW 2673, qui aurait percuté un pick-up appartenant à une société intervenant sur le chantier du barrage hydroélectrique d’Amaria. D’après les mêmes témoignages, cinq personnes se trouvaient à bord du pick-up, dont ce travailleur expatrié qui a perdu la vie sur place. Les autres, grièvement blessés, ont été évacués d’urgence vers l’hôpital préfectoral de Dubréka pour recevoir des soins. Naby Laye Fofana, l’un des chauffeurs présents sur les lieux, a confirmé le décès sur le champ de ce travailleur étranger ainsi que la présence des autres blessés. Il explique avoir été informé très tôt dans la matinée et avoir constaté les conséquences de l’accident à son arrivée sur place. L’officier chargé du constat, présent sur les lieux, a également confirmé les faits. Une source sanitaire de l’hôpital préfectoral de Dubréka a, de son côté, confirmé la prise en charge des accidentés ainsi que la présence du corps de la victime à l’hopital. Au moment où nous quittions les lieux, les agents de sécurité étaient mobilisés afin de sécuriser la zone et de faciliter le rétablissement de la circulation. Les circonstances exactes de l’accident restent à déterminer par les services compétents.

items.title: Sandbondtenga/Développement: La Délégation spéciale de Boussouma réaménage son budget 2026
items.description: BURKINA-SANDBONDTENGA-BOUSSOUMA-DÉVELOPPEMENT – BUDGET Sandbondtenga/Développement: La Délégation spéciale de Boussouma réaménage son budget 2026 Boussouma, 9 sept. 2026 (AIB)-La Délégation spéciale de la commune de Boussouma a adopté mercredi 9 septembre 2026, à l’unanimité, le deuxième budget rectificatif au titre de l’exercice 2026, au cours de sa troisième session ordinaire, portant son budget global à 628329227 Fcfa. Cette session de la Délégation spéciale qui a enregistré la présence des chefs de service de la mairie, a permis d’examiner et d’adopter le deuxième budget rectificatif. Un réajustement budgétaire en vue d'assurer la poursuite des activités et le fonctionnement de la commune dans un contexte marqué par des défis de développement. Le budget primitif 2026 de la commune s’élevait à 252 190 936 F CFA, avant d’être porté à 628329227 Fcfa soit 219695328 F CFA en fonctionnement et 500339928 F CFA en investissement à la faveur des budgets rectificatifs. Pour le deuxième budget rectificatif, a été adopté à l’unanimité à 40963165 soit 40963165 en fonctionnement et 29192633 en investissement. Pour le deuxième budget rectificatif, les crédits prévus concernent notamment 20 963 165 F CFA au titre du fonctionnement et 9 192 633 F CFA pour l’investissement. Présentant le contexte de la session, Madjoa Lompo, président de la délégation spéciale communale a relevé la pression exercée sur les services sociaux de base, la baisse des activités économiques et les difficultés de mobilisation des recettes locales. Les orientations budgétaires et les engagements portent notamment sur l’entretien des infrastructures communales, le désenclavement des villages, l’accompagnement des jeunes et l’amélioration de l’accès aux services sociaux de base. La session a également permis aux membres de la Délégation spéciale communale de s'approprier les principales orientations budgétaires pour 2027, axées sur le renforcement de la résilience communautaire, la cohésion sociale, la gouvernance participative, la recherche de financements et la réalisation des projets prioritaires de la commune. Plusieurs délibérations ont été prises portant notamment sur l'ouverture d’un concours professionnel destiné aux fonctionnaires communaux, l'autorisation de signature de convention avec l’Agence nationale d’appui au développement des collectivités territoriales (ANAC) dans le cadre de l’offre de bourses au profit des agents des collectivités territoriales pour l’édition 2026-2028.
